value.text: A 24-year-old woman has died from injuries she suffered after she was struck while riding an electric scooter in a hit-and-run crash in Port St. Lucie, police said Wednesday.The woman died at approximately 9:23 p.m. Tuesday, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The crash happened around 5:10 a.m. Monday near the intersection of Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace.Police said the woman was riding an electric scooter when a vehicle struck her. Investigators allege the driver left the scene without stopping to help her or notify law enforcement.The department's Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit later identified the vehicle as a gray Chevrolet Tahoe and located it at a Port St. Lucie home, according to police.Investigators identified the alleged driver as 18-year-old Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer.Police said investigators learned Sanchez-Chasmer had been playing "ding dong ditch" with friends shortly before the crash. According to the department, the group was leaving a home where they had been participating in the prank when the vehicle struck the woman.Sanchez-Chasmer was arrested and charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, a second-degree felony, police said.Following the woman's death, police said they anticipate the State Attorney's Office will pursue enhanced or additional charges as appropriate based on the circumstances and the outcome of the investigation.Police did not identify the woman in Wednesday's news release.

A new 24/7 animal cruelty hotline in Florida is already getting results just hours after its launch was announced.Big Dog Ranch Rescue CEO and founder Lauree Simmons said the hotline went live Monday, and the organization received more than 30 calls. It also led to the rescue of an abandoned and neglected dog in Bay County.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The hotline gives people a place to report suspected animal abuse, including cruelty, abandonment and dog fighting. The reports are then turned over to law enforcement, animal control or a government agency for possible investigation."These animals can't call — you can. You see an animal being neglected, starved, call and report it," Simmons said.The Florida Statewide Animal Cruelty Hotline is operated by Big Dog Ranch Rescue, located in Loxahatchee Groves, and funded through the state. The hotline number is 844-4-SOSPET (844-476-7738). People can report anonymously, and it's available 24/7.Click here to read more about the hotline.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

A massive indoor pickleball facility is opening its doors in Boca Raton.Boca Paddle by City Pickle is officially welcoming players to 25 brand-new courts. It's the city's first fully climate-controlled indoor pickleball and padel club.Day passes cost $40, with Boca Raton residents getting $5 off. The center also features a restaurant and bar, a shop, and fitness and recovery spaces like a sauna and cold plunge. One of its co-founders says Boca Paddle is unlike anything else in the city. Boca Raton's mayor says the city is the right fit for this type of facility.The area that we're in right now, here in North Park, is in need of revitalization. And this facility, by itself, takes a huge step in that direction to help revitalize this part of the city," Boca Raton Mayor Andy Thomson said.The facility will also be the home of a new professional team."I'm excited that we're a home for the Palm Beach Royals, which is major league pickleball's newest franchise. They paid $16 million last year. They're going to be based here," Boca Paddle Co-Founder Brian Levine said.By the numbers, the facility spans 100,000 square feet and cost around $20 million to build. It has 14 indoor pickleball courts and nine outdoor courts, along with two padel courts.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

The School District of Palm Beach County has canceled all after-school activities Wednesday due to the afternoon weather forecast.All schools and district offices remain open Wednesday, Nov. 18, the district said.The cancellations include athletic events, clubs, meetings, Adult Workforce and Community Education classes and leases.Aftercare programs will remain open until 4 p.m. Families with children in aftercare are being asked to pick them up by that time.The district is also encouraging families to monitor their children's bus routes in real time through the free Here Comes the Bus app.District officials said they are monitoring the forecast for Thursday, Nov. 19, and plan to provide an update later Wednesday about school operations.The district said student and staff safety remains its top priority as officials continue to monitor weather conditions.

People are sacrificing their long-term savings to afford the holidays this year. A new survey of 1,000 people by USA Capitol Gold found 42% of Americans plan to cut back on or draw from their savings and investments to afford holiday expenses. WATCH: New survey shows people plan to dig into savings to afford holiday purchasesNearly 1 in 5 say they expect to take on debt to cover holiday costs. Of those who plan to take on debt, 16% of those surveyed say they plan to charge it to their credit card, whereas 10% say they'll rely on buy now, pay later options to make purchases.The poll set out to understand how rising costs and economic pressures are affecting consumers' savings, retirement plans, investment decisions, and long-term financial goals. The study also reflects a growing habit of more people investing less money each month to pay for everyday expenses.Click here to read the full study.

The South Florida Water Management District has issued an emergency order allowing certain pumping and water-management measures as communities contend with saturated ground and the threat of additional heavy rainfall.The emergency final order, signed by Executive Director Drew Bartlett, is intended to help address flooding caused by the heavy rainfall that has hit portions of Florida beginning Oct. The district said some impacted areas received more than 10 inches of rain in 36 hours, causing widespread flooding and leaving standing water and saturated ground. WATCH BELOW: Flood victims worried as Martin County braces for more rainThe order comes as additional localized heavy rain threatens areas already hit hard by flooding. The district said those conditions create an "imminent threat" of additional significant flooding and damage to life and property. The emergency action stems from state-of-emergency declarations issued by Gov. 4 in response to the flooding. Under the order, water can be moved from flooded portions of a property, including roadways, parking lots and swales, to ponds, lakes or other areas on the same property without notifying the district, as long as the water is not being discharged off-site. Moving floodwater off-site requires more oversight. The district must approve such discharges after a field inspection, and the flooding must pose an immediate threat to public health, safety or welfare. The order specifically says minor flooding, such as standing water in roads, swales or yards, does not qualify as an immediate threat. Local governments and water control districts can also receive authorization to discharge water beyond their normal district-permitted operating schedules to prepare for or reduce flooding. They must notify the district's Emergency Operations Center and receive authorization from district staff. WATCH BELOW: Flooding threat collides with St. Lucie County budget concernsThe district said all emergency activities must be carried out in ways that minimize impacts to water quality and quantity. Those carrying out pumping or discharges must also correct any erosion, sediment or water-quality problems resulting from the work. The order temporarily suspends certain permitting and notice requirements when necessary for the specifically authorized emergency activities. However, it does not eliminate requirements imposed by other federal, state or local agencies. The emergency order took effect immediately upon its execution and is scheduled to expire Jan. 1, 2027, unless it is extended or ended earlier by the district's executive director or Governing Board.The district said its emergency operations center remains at Level 2 partial activation. They also remind everyone to avoid floodwaters resulting from heavy rains. If you face life-threatening flooding or are in imminent danger, call 9-1-1Avoid driving through flooded areas. When in doubt, turn aroundEnsure debris, trash cans, and other items are secured and cannot blow into drainage ways Monitor announcements from your County Emergency Operations CenterFloodwaters can hide hidden dangers. Just two weeks after historic flooding forced schools to close for three straight days, St. Lucie County students are getting another day off as more heavy rain threatens the area. Lucie Public Schools announced Tuesday that all schools and district offices will be closed Wednesday due to the threat of significant rainfall and localized flooding. The announcement comes after the district dismissed students two hours early Tuesday as worsening weather conditions raised concerns about flooding. It's the latest disruption for the district, which was forced to close schools for three consecutive days Nov. 4, 5 and 6 after historic flooding left roads underwater and communities struggling to recover. Lucie County clears drains, prepares for more rain after historic flooding Now, with the ground already saturated, district leaders say they aren't taking any chances. According to the district, forecasts from the National Weather Service indicate the potential for significant rainfall, although uncertainty remains about exactly when and where the heaviest rain will fall. "Given the already saturated conditions in our community, the District believes taking a cautious approach is in the best interest of our students, families, and employees," district officials said in a statement. John Carroll High School also announced it will be closed Wednesday, Nov. 18, due to the threat of heavy rainfall and flooding across the region. The decision follows an early dismissal Tuesday and a review of weather forecasts and local flooding conditions. School officials said all Wednesday activities, including athletics, practices, extracurricular programs and other events, have been canceled. John Carroll anticipates reopening Thursday, pending weather and road conditions. Administrators will continue monitoring forecasts and coordinating with local authorities before making further decisions. Updates will be shared through the school's official communication channels. All after-school activities, aftercare programs, and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday have also been canceled. District officials said they will continue monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures, and access to schools, bus stops, and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision on whether schools will reopen Thursday is expected Wednesday evening. Families are encouraged to monitor the district's official website and social media channels for updates.

An 18-year-old driver has been arrested after Port St. Lucie Police Department investigators say he struck a 24-year-old woman riding an electric scooter to work and left the scene, leaving her critically injured. Police say the driver had been playing a "ding-dong-ditch" prank with friends shortly before Monday morning's crash.WATCH: E-Scooter Hit-and-Run in Port St. LuciePolice identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer. He was arrested on a felony charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, according to the department.The crash happened near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Investigators said the woman was traveling west on the sidewalk toward Southwest Rosser Boulevard and had entered a crosswalk when she was hit by a gray Chevrolet Tahoe making a left turn onto Southwest Feather Terrace.Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said Tuesday the woman remained unconscious and in critical condition."We're deeply concerned for her recovery, and our thoughts are with her loved ones," Niemczyk said.Police said a witness stopped to help the woman, called 911 and was able to get the SUV's license plate information. Investigators used that information to identify the vehicle and the driver. Investigators said Sanchez-Chasmer had two friends with him and had been playing "ding-dong-ditch" shortly before the crash. "They were specifically playing, I'll call it ring and run, ding-dong-ditch, at a house that belonged to a friend of theirs, and apparently the mother came to the door and they fled the scene," Niemczyk told WPTV.Niemczyk said investigators believe the people inside the SUV realized a collision had occurred."They're aware that they hit something. I'll say that," he said.According to Niemczyk, Sanchez-Chasmer and the two passengers did not call 911.Niemczyk said the decision to leave the scene was key to the criminal investigation."Had they remained on scene, provided aid, it would have been a very different criminal outcome," Niemczyk said. "There probably wouldn't have been criminal charges at that point."Sanchez-Chasmer was charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. According to published reports citing law enforcement records, he was being held on a $5,000 bond. Police have not announced charges against the two passengers. WPTV returned to the intersection after the crash and spoke with 15-year-old John Rogalewski, who said he rides an e-scooter to school and is sometimes on the road early in the morning."I'm looking at my surroundings almost the whole time," Rogalewski said. "I'm making sure every time I have to cross the street that there's not a car coming up, and that it is my sign to go, no matter how long I have to wait to cross."Police said the 24-year-old woman was wearing a helmet when she was struck.The investigation remains active, according to police, and toxicology results are still pending.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Residents in Riviera Beach are preparing for another round of rain weeks after floodwaters damaged or destroyed hundreds of homes, including properties in Lone Pine Estates. With families still recovering, residents lined up for sandbags Tuesday as city leaders worked to identify financial assistance for homeowners.For families who recently watched water enter their homes, the possibility of more rain is bringing back fears of another flood.WATCH: Riviera Beach residents brace for more rain after devastating floodsResidents prepare for more rainWPTV saw a line of cars as residents waited to pick up sandbags, with neighbors shoveling sand and loading bags into their vehicles.“Keeping my fingers crossed,” said Keisha Harty while preparing for the rain.WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache reconnected with the Harty family, who were waiting in line for sandbags while still recovering from the previous flooding.“We need sandbags to put in front, just in case,” Harty said. “I don’t want another flood. Not another one again.”Lone Pine Estates was among the Riviera Beach communities hit by the recent flooding, which left hundreds of homes damaged or destroyed.Homeowner Guy Volel said his house flooded on consecutive days.“Last week my house got flooded both days,” Volel said. “All the stuff inside my house is falling apart.”Riviera Beach considers $2 million relief proposalThe preparations come after an emergency meeting Monday night as residents continued pressing city leaders for help.Riviera Beach Mayor Douglas Lawson told WPTV that city officials are looking for ways to get financial assistance to affected homeowners.“Residents are hurting and we’re trying to find every vehicle to help them to get the resources they need to rebuild their homes,” Lawson said.City leaders are considering a $2 million relief proposal for residents affected by the flooding. Lawson said officials directed staff to move quickly and hoped to have more information before the Thanksgiving break.“We demanded that staff comes back as quickly as possible,” Lawson said. “So hopefully by next week, prior to the Thanksgiving break, we’ll have some answers for our residents to be able to disseminate some of this money we’ve allocated for them.”City hopes for federal disaster assistanceLawson said the city is also hoping for a major disaster declaration from the president that could make federal disaster assistance available to residents.“Emotions are high because residents lost everything,” Lawson said.For residents preparing their homes once again, the focus is now on preventing more damage while they wait for answers about financial assistance.“We’re here with you, we’re praying for you and we’re supporting you,” Lawson said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Due to anticipated rainfall, at least one public-school district and a private school on the Treasure Coast will close. LUCIE COUNTY A spokesperson for the St. Lucie County Public Schools announced that the school district will be closed to students and employees on Wednesday, Nov. "While there remains some uncertainty regarding the exact timing, location, and amount of rainfall, current forecasts from the National Weather Service indicate the potential for significant rainfall and localized flooding. Given the already saturated conditions in our community, the District believes taking a cautious approach is in the best interest of our students, families, and employees," the school district spokesperson said in a statement. All after-school activities, after-care programs and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday were canceled. The spokesperson added that school district officials will continue to monitor rainfall, flooding, road closures and the accessibility of schools, bus stops and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision about school reopening on Thursday will be announced on Wednesday evening. The school district said it will provide updates on its website and social media platforms. John Carroll High School: The private school in Fort Pierce announced it will be closed on Wednesday because of the potential for heavy rainfall and flooding throughout the region. "The decision follows today's early dismissal and a review of current weather forecasts and local flooding conditions. School officials determined that closing campus is the best course of action to ensure the safety of students, faculty, staff, and families," the school said in a statement to WPBF 25 News on Tuesday evening. "All school-sponsored activities scheduled for Wednesday, including athletics, practices, extracurricular programs, and other events, have been canceled." The school added it anticipates resuming normal operations on Thursday, Nov. 19, pending weather and road conditions. "Administrators will continue to monitor forecasts and remain in communication with local authorities before making any further decisions regarding school operations," the school said. "Updates will be shared through the school’s official communication channels as conditions warrant." Boys Girls Club of Palm Beach County: All Boys Girls Club school sites in Palm Beach County are closed November 18 due to weather concerns, while other club sites remain open. Lucie County: All after-school programs and Clubhouse locations will be closed on Wednesday, Nov. MARTIN COUNTY The Martin County School District said that school and Extended Day will be open to students on Wednesday, but all other after-school activities, athletic practices and events are canceled for Wednesday. Officials in Martin County will monitor weather conditions. Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County: All Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County locations will reopen on Wednesday, Nov. 18, and resume normal operating hours. INDIAN RIVER COUNTY The School District of Indian River County announced on Tuesday afternoon that there will be a regular school schedule for students and employees, including Extended Day and extracurricular activities, on Wednesday, Nov. "District teams found no standing water affecting safe routes to bus stops. Families are encouraged to make the best decision for their circumstances," a spokesperson for the school district said in a statement on Tuesday. "Weather-related absences will follow standard attendance procedures and will not be excused solely due to weather." Democrat Mary Peltola is projected to defeat Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, according to the Associated Press, delivering a significant pickup for Democrats.ANALYSIS | The significance of Peltola's election winPeltola's victory marks the first time since 2008 that a Democrat has won a U.S. Senate election in Alaska, and gives Democrats a 56-44 majority in the Senate — though two lawmakers identify as Independents and simply caucus with the Democrats."As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first," Peltola said in a statement. "As our next United States Senator, I will stand up to anyone to take on the rigged system in DC and deliver results for Alaska’s working families. Let’s get to work.”Peltola, who made history in 2022 as the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, focused her Senate campaign on lowering the cost of living and addressing economic challenges facing everyday Alaskans.She previously served in the U.S. House of Representatives, where she became known for emphasizing issues important to Alaska, including the state's fishing industry and economic development.The race drew national attention as Republicans fought to defend their Senate majority. Sullivan, a military veteran seeking a third term, received support from President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance.Sullivan aligned his campaign with the Trump administration's tax and spending priorities and advocated for expanding fossil fuel production.The race in Alaska was complicated by the presence of another Dan Sullivan on the ballot. Sullivan, a retired teacher, ran as a long shot Democratic candidate for Senate. Both Dan Sullivans running prompted a legal fight early in the campaign, and President Donald Trump later called the former teacher's campaign "fake" and "a hoax by the Democrats."

The Treasure Coast is bracing for a soggy stretch as counties prepare for possible flooding from heavy rain. Indian River County The Indian River County Emergency Operations Center remains at Level 2, or partial activation, because of ongoing flooding and the potential for more heavy rain. Emergency services, human services and infrastructure partners are coordinating response and recovery efforts. The county urges residents to avoid flooded roads and floodwaters, watch for rising water in low-lying areas and monitor weather conditions and official updates. Residents with flood-related questions or information can call the Emergency Information Center at 772-226-4000 during operating hours. Due to the heavy rain and gusty winds, solid waste services may be disrupted. Waste Management curbside collections may be delayed, and residents should not put carts in the street if it is flooded. See also: Florida deputies rescue 2-year-old girl found in pond near apartment complex Waste Management collects recycling in blue carts countywide. It collects garbage, yard waste and bulk waste in unincorporated Indian River County, Fellsmere, Sebastian and Indian River Shores. Residents in other cities and towns should check with their local governments for service updates. The county recommends putting carts out by 6 a.m. on collection day, closing lids, bagging garbage, and avoiding overfilled carts. Cardboard should be flattened and placed inside recycling carts, and yard waste should stay inside yard waste carts. Residents should bring carts back in as soon as possible after collection. The landfill and all five Customer Convenience Centers may close early or remain closed if conditions become unsafe. The east-central Florida coast faces a Slight Risk, or Level 2 out of 4, for excessive rainfall. Localized flooding is possible, especially along the coast, and some areas could receive 4 inches or more of rain. Martin County Martin County officials expect 3 to 6 inches of rain, with localized amounts of 8 to 12 inches, beginning Tuesday afternoon and continuing through Nov. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office says it is working with the county’s emergency operations center to monitor rainfall and identify roads that could become difficult to pass. The sheriff’s office plans to deploy high-water rescue vehicles in flood-prone areas. Having the vehicles nearby could help deputies reach residents who need assistance and motorists who become stranded, the office said. The sheriff’s office advises residents to turn around if water covers the road. Standing water may be deeper than it appears and can hide damage. If a regular route is flooded, drivers should take another route or wait somewhere safe. Residents should never drive around barricades or enter flooded areas to see how high the water is. Martin County Fire Rescue also advises residents to be prepared to evacuate if flooding threatens their homes or neighborhoods and to have an emergency kit ready for household members and pets. The Community Information Center will be open to provide flood-related information. Okeechobee County Okeechobee County is also preparing for severe flooding. The Okeechobee County Sheriff’s Office says its emergency operations center will remain active as staff coordinate response and recovery efforts from past flooding. Sandbags are available at Okeechobee County Public Works, 804 Northwest Second St. Lucie County Public Safety Department is monitoring the forecast and reminding residents to secure loose items that could be damaged by wind. Gusty northeast winds of 25 to 30 mph are forecast Tuesday and Wednesday, with gusts of 35 to 40 mph along the coast. Residents should secure tarps, patio furniture and other unsecured items. A rip current advisory remains in effect for St. Strong onshore winds can create dangerous rip currents and rough surf. Lucie County Fire District says its firefighters, paramedics and telecommunicators are prepared to respond as the area faces more heavy rain and recovers from recent flooding. The district has high-water vehicles and a rescue boat available to assist during flood-related emergencies. Free sand is available while supplies last at two self-service locations: County Fairgrounds: 5601 W. Midway Road, Fort Pierce, in the west parking lot Lawnwood Stadium: 2000 Virginia Ave., Fort Pierce Residents should bring their own bags, shovel and other supplies. Residents can use Community Connect to share household information that could help firefighters prepare for an emergency. The county has extended the deadline to Nov. 30 for residents to report flood damage through an online survey. The information will help document flooding across the community and inform recovery efforts. The survey is open to property owners and tenants throughout St. Lucie County, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated areas. It asks where flooding occurred, how buildings were affected and what impacts residents and businesses experienced. Residents can complete the flood damage survey by Nov. Officials urge residents across the region to avoid flooded roads and keep roadways clear for emergency responders. If you encounter flooding, turn around and find a safe alternate route.

Crews are clearing drainage systems and checking waterways in St. Lucie County as another round of rain threatens areas still recovering from historic flooding. Lucie Public Schools is releasing students two hours early Tuesday. The district announced Tuesday afternoon that schools and offices will be closed Wednesday as a precaution. All after-school activities, aftercare programs, and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are also canceled. District officials will continue monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures, and the accessibility of schools, bus stops, and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision regarding school operations for Thursday, November 19, will be announced Wednesday evening. Lucie officials say Public Works crews are inspecting drainage systems, clearing blockages and lowering water levels where possible. The ground remains saturated, increasing the risk of flooding even if rainfall is lighter than it was during the early November storms. See also: Heavy rain returns this week, bringing major threat of flooding across South Florida The National Weather Service has issued a flood watch for St. Lucie County from Tuesday afternoon through Friday evening. Forecasters expect 3 to 6 inches of rain across the area, with higher amounts possible in some locations. Two weeks ago, floodwaters stranded cars, trapped families and forced some residents to wade through deep water. Videos from that flooding showed high school freshman Noah Julian swimming from his school bus toward his home in a flooded Port St. Another video showed 7-year-old Ella Ghodooshim walking through chest-deep water with her mother near Oak Hammock K-8. That mother, Thassia Rodrigues, told CBS12 her only concern was getting her daughter safely across the flooded intersection. "As long as I can get her across and get her to safety, that was my main concern," Rodrigues said. She described how quickly the flooding overwhelmed the neighborhood, leaving parents struggling to reach their children. "It was pretty scary and in a matter of minutes we had everything just flood," she said. Lucie Public Schools told CBS12 News that decisions about closures and early dismissal are based on forecasts and information from the National Weather Service and Emergency Operations Center. The district said the information available before the previous flooding did not indicate schools needed to close or dismiss students earlier. This time, officials said the forecast supported releasing students two hours early to get them home before the heaviest rain. The district said it was awaiting additional updates from the National Weather Service at 2 p.m. and Emergency Operations Center at 4 p.m. Tuesday before making any further decisions about school schedules. Parents picking up their children near Oak Hammock K-8 Tuesday told CBS12 News they welcomed the earlier dismissal. "It's kind of nice that they're doing it early so we have time to get them and not have to rush," said Nathan Leach, whose child attends the school. Rhett Linton, another parent, recalled kayaking through the flooded intersection during the previous storm. "I'm super happy that they are stepping up and taking precautions," Linton said. Rodrigues, who was captured on video helping her daughter through the floodwaters, also praised the district's decision. Lucie County, we appreciate you guys," she said. Officials are urging residents to plan ahead, monitor forecasts and local alerts, and limit unnecessary travel. Drivers should never enter standing or moving water. Floodwater can stall a vehicle and cause costly engine damage. If you cannot tell how deep the water is, turn around and find another route. Residents can report flooding concerns to St. Lucie County at flooding@stlucieco.org .

Lucie Public Schools will dismiss students two hours early Tuesday as rain moves into the area, with heavier rainfall possible in the evening. The district said it made the decision as a precaution based on information from the National Weather Service . Parents and guardians are encouraged to consider conditions in their neighborhoods. Absences caused by weather will be excused, the district said. Heavier rain is possible Wednesday through Friday and could lead to school closures. The district is monitoring conditions with the St. Lucie County Emergency Operations Center and the National Weather Service. The district said it will announce any changes to Tuesday’s after-school activities and athletics based on weather conditions. Families should check the district’s official channels for updates. Neighboring Indian River County schools will also operate on a modified schedule Tuesday, Nov. 17, with students dismissed early, according to the School District of Indian River County. The district announced the following dismissal times: High schools: 12:20 p.m. Middle schools and K-8: 1 p.m. Elementary schools: 1:50 p.m. Wabasso School: 12:30 p.m. Morning arrival times will remain unchanged, and transportation will operate as normal during early dismissal. Extended Day will be available Tuesday morning but closed in the afternoon. All extracurricular activities must conclude by 2:30 p.m. The district said additional updates will be shared as information becomes available. RELATED: Heavy rain returns this week, bringing major threat of flooding across south Florida Palm Beach County schools are still scheduled to open Tuesday, Nov. The district will continue monitoring the weather and share updates if anything changes. Okeechobee County schools will also be open. Martin County schools will also remain open Tuesday; however, all after-school activities will be cancelled. The ground is already soaked from the rain we experienced the first weekend of the month, so it won't take much to create flooding concerns. Right now, up to 4-5 inches of rain is possible, but higher isolated amounts can't be ruled out.

Please make the decision that is safest for your family. If weather conditions prevent your child from attending school, the absence will be excused,” the school district announced in a statement on Monday. On Monday, the National Weather Service issued a flood watch for Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties beginning on Tuesday afternoon through Friday evening. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. After isolated and scattered showers on Monday, rain chances increase on Tuesday with scattered showers and a few thunderstorms. There is a chance of heavy rainfall. On Wednesday, widespread showers, storms and rainfall are forecast while flooding is possible.

Lucie County Schools Superintendent Dr. Jon Prince apologized to the district Tuesday night and promised a review of all decisions and actions from the historic flooding on Nov. "It was very stressful for our families, and I certainly apologize for the stress that they went through on that day," Prince said. A video from that day shows a boy getting off a school bus on SW Coleman Avenue in Port St. Lucie and walking through flood waters that reach as high as his chest. Critics have pointed to that video and questioned the actions of the school district. In an exclusive interview, Prince expressed regret over the events of Nov. 2, stating that decisions were made based on the information available at the time. He emphasized that the flooding was unexpected. "The bottom line is I don't know of anything that could have predicted what transpired as the day progressed," Prince said. Prince assured that every decision made that day is being analyzed. "We are going to review all our procedures, our policies to make sure that if there's anything that we could have done differently, that moving forward we will," he said. With heavy rain in the forecast, St. Lucie County Schools decided to cancel classes for Wednesday. Prince said he hopes the decision is an overreaction. At the same time, though, he does not want to take any chances. "The ground is so saturated, but if the conditions worsen tomorrow, we don't want a repeat of what happened November 2," Prince said. Prince said the district will monitor the weather Wednesday and decide late Wednesday afternoon if classes should be canceled again Thursday. He said they'll follow that model until they are sure it's safe for students to return to class. An 18-year-old driver has been arrested after Port St. Lucie Police Department investigators say he struck a 24-year-old woman riding an electric scooter to work and left the scene, leaving her critically injured. Police say the driver had been playing a "ding-dong-ditch" prank with friends shortly before Monday morning's crash.WATCH: E-Scooter Hit-and-Run in Port St. LuciePolice identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer. He was arrested on a felony charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, according to the department.The crash happened near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Investigators said the woman was traveling west on the sidewalk toward Southwest Rosser Boulevard and had entered a crosswalk when she was hit by a gray Chevrolet Tahoe making a left turn onto Southwest Feather Terrace.Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said Tuesday the woman remained unconscious and in critical condition."We're deeply concerned for her recovery, and our thoughts are with her loved ones," Niemczyk said.Police said a witness stopped to help the woman, called 911 and was able to get the SUV's license plate information. Investigators used that information to identify the vehicle and the driver. Investigators said Sanchez-Chasmer had two friends with him and had been playing "ding-dong-ditch" shortly before the crash. "They were specifically playing, I'll call it ring and run, ding-dong-ditch, at a house that belonged to a friend of theirs, and apparently the mother came to the door and they fled the scene," Niemczyk told WPTV.Niemczyk said investigators believe the people inside the SUV realized a collision had occurred."They're aware that they hit something. I'll say that," he said.According to Niemczyk, Sanchez-Chasmer and the two passengers did not call 911.Niemczyk said the decision to leave the scene was key to the criminal investigation."Had they remained on scene, provided aid, it would have been a very different criminal outcome," Niemczyk said. "There probably wouldn't have been criminal charges at that point."Sanchez-Chasmer was charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. According to published reports citing law enforcement records, he was being held on a $5,000 bond. Police have not announced charges against the two passengers. WPTV returned to the intersection after the crash and spoke with 15-year-old John Rogalewski, who said he rides an e-scooter to school and is sometimes on the road early in the morning."I'm looking at my surroundings almost the whole time," Rogalewski said. "I'm making sure every time I have to cross the street that there's not a car coming up, and that it is my sign to go, no matter how long I have to wait to cross."Police said the 24-year-old woman was wearing a helmet when she was struck.The investigation remains active, according to police, and toxicology results are still pending.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. An 18-year-old is under arrest after police say he was playing a game of ding, dong, ditch with some friends and then hit a woman on an e-scooter and drove away. Police have identified the driver as Tristan Ray Sanchez-Chasmer, 18, of Port St. "Pranks especially at somebody's front door, especially at late hours of the night, early hours of the morning can be very dangerous," said Leo Niemczyk, Port St. Lucie Police say the crash happened Monday, November 16, at about 5:10 am near the intersection of SW Gatlin Blvd. and SW Feather Terrace in Port St. Police say a 24 year old woman on an e-scooter was hit by a vehicle that did not stop. The victim was on her way to a Wendy's where she works and she was in the crosswalk on SW Feather Terrace when she was hit. "I think for somebody to just leave another human being on the side of the road who was possibly injured, to not stop and check on them, it's truly heartbreaking that somebody would make that decision," said Katie Santana, a Port St. Lucie resident who lives near the intersection where the accident happened. We spoke with a high school student who rides an e-scooter in the area where the crash occurred. "I get a little bit fearful sometimes, 'cause I'll see some people going through red lights, not paying attention when they're turning and I've almost been hit a couple times," said John Rogalewski, age 15. See also: Bodycam footage shows deputy fatally shoot armed Florida mother, army veteran outside bar Police say a good Samaritan got the license plate number of the hit and run vehicle and stopped to help the victim. With that information, police determined a Chevy Tahoe struck the woman, and they determined the driver was an 18-year-old. Sanchez-Chasmer is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. Police say the victim was rushed to a hospital and, at last report, she was hospitalized in critical condition. Police say she is in a coma. If she does not survive, the State Attorney's Office would decide if Sanchez-Chasmer could face a more serious charge. Police say two other individuals who were in the Chevy Tahoe with Sanchez-Chasmer have not been charged.

A 24-year-old woman has died from injuries she suffered after she was struck while riding an electric scooter in a hit-and-run crash in Port St. Lucie, police said Wednesday.The woman died at approximately 9:23 p.m. Tuesday, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The crash happened around 5:10 a.m. Monday near the intersection of Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace.Police said the woman was riding an electric scooter when a vehicle struck her. Investigators allege the driver left the scene without stopping to help her or notify law enforcement.The department's Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit later identified the vehicle as a gray Chevrolet Tahoe and located it at a Port St. Lucie home, according to police.Investigators identified the alleged driver as 18-year-old Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer.Police said investigators learned Sanchez-Chasmer had been playing "ding dong ditch" with friends shortly before the crash. According to the department, the group was leaving a home where they had been participating in the prank when the vehicle struck the woman.Sanchez-Chasmer was arrested and charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, a second-degree felony, police said.Following the woman's death, police said they anticipate the State Attorney's Office will pursue enhanced or additional charges as appropriate based on the circumstances and the outcome of the investigation.Police did not identify the woman in Wednesday's news release.

Parents could face criminal charges in a crackdown on illegal e-bikes after a teen was thrown 50 feet in a crash, the Martin County sheriff warned Monday. During a news conference, the sheriff revealed that a 14-year-old Port St. Lucie boy suffered catastrophic injuries in Sunday's crash near U.S. 1 and Northwest Goldenrod Road. The teen was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center , where he is now in stable condition. According to the sheriff, the boy and a friend had traveled roughly five miles from home on separate e-bikes when they attempted to cross U.S. See also: Kids, 6,000 fentanyl pills and stolen gun uncovered in massive Florida drug bust The first teen made it across, but the 14-year-old was struck by a northbound vehicle that had a green light. The impact sent the boy flying approximately 50 feet, while his e-bike landed about 100 feet away. "Had he not been wearing a helmet, and had he been hit just a little different, we'd be talking about a 14-year-old die in a fatality crash," the sheriff said. Investigators determined the teen was riding a 3,300-watt electric bike, more than four times the 750-watt limit cited by the sheriff. The motorbike-style vehicle was not street-legal, he said. The crash comes amid growing concerns over e-bike safety in Martin County, where the sheriff reported 41 e-bike crashes this year, involving riders as young as 7 and as old as 80. The sheriff said educational workshops, warnings, and previous enforcement efforts have failed to curb dangerous riding. Now, deputies are considering tougher consequences, including seizing illegal e-bikes and potentially pursuing criminal charges against parents who knowingly allow their children to ride them. I'm not anti-e-bikes, but I'm anti-illegal e-bikes being ridden irresponsibly on our streets." The Florida Highway Patrol is leading the crash investigation, with assistance from the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

After back-to-back 1,000-yard receiving seasons, FAU wide receiver Easton Messer is on several NFL Draft boards and looks to be the Owls' first draft pick in six years.I sat down with the FAU Owls standout for a one-on-one conversation about his journey — one that spanned multiple countries before leading him to South Florida.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Messer moved around a lot over the years."My first place was Costa Rica, then I moved back to Louisville, then Panama, and lastly Malaysia," Messer said.Growing up, he played both soccer and American football — a combination he credits with shaping his footwork and technique."I really haven't thought about the fact that soccer helped out my feet and helped me play receiver, but soccer is big pretty much everywhere but the U.S. Just being over in those places and trying to get integrated into the culture," Messer said.Football, though, was always his sport."Growing up, that was my sport. I played football, basketball and a little bit of baseball, but football was my favorite one. I went to high school at Christian Academy in Louisville," Messer said.In high school, Messer was a standout receiver but felt he was under-recruited."It was pretty short; it wasn't a ton of recruiting with me being undersized and not passing the eye test. I had a couple offers, and I wasn't sure if they were commitable, and I ended up having to walk on at Western Kentucky," Messer said.After standing out over three years at Western Kentucky, Messer entered the transfer portal and ultimately arrived at FAU."My transfer portal recruitment wasn't really popping either; not a lot of people reached out," Messer said.Since 2020, no Owls player has heard their name called in the NFL Draft. Messer could change that in a few months."Personally, for me, going from a walk-on and not really getting recruited to possibly getting my name called on draft night, it doesn't even feel real at this point, but we got some other guys too," Messer said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. As the threat of another round of November rain and flooding takes aim at Florida's east coast, many local governments are once again preparing for what may be ahead. "I think everybody is well aware now that this storm drain system was not designed for the flooding we're getting nowadays," St. Lucie County spokesman Erick Gill said.WATCH REPORT BELOW: He said crews are being deployed across the county as they were two weeks ago. "There were probably 50 to 100 staff members out there, including crews in public works, out in the field working during the storm. That's unbudgeted overtime," Gill said. This week, the county offered free sand, donated by Dickerson Infrastructure and Stewart Materials, for residents to bag. Other services cost money, and Gill said budgeting is already on the minds of county leaders now that the Amendment 3 tax cuts are coming. What is uncertain is how the loss of revenue will affect things like storm preparation and response. "We still don't know what the total impacts will be for, you know, with Amendment 3 with the additional homestead exemption," Gill said. "We're looking at the early estimates in this next upcoming fiscal year to be about a $60 million shortfall and then about $120 million once the exemption goes up."

A historic Vero Beach neighborhood is getting a new life through art, as sculptor Ross Power leads an effort to transform Edgewood into a vibrant community of artists, galleries, studios and public gathering spaces.Known as the "Father of the Vero Beach Art Village," Power is helping turn a once-overlooked neighborhood into a destination for creativity, where artists can live, work and share their talents.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The transformation is already underway, with murals, public art and community projects taking shape. Power says more galleries, studios, cafes and bed-and-breakfasts are in the works, bringing new opportunities for artists, residents and visitors.A historic Vero Beach neighborhood becomes a canvasUnder the shade of a century-old lychee tree, Power reads from a poem dedicated to the tree as a dancer performs beneath its branches."A place where you and me can become we," Power said.For the longtime sculptor, the tree represents something bigger: a gathering place where art can bring people together.That vision is unfolding in Edgewood, a neighborhood established in 1916 that was once home to Vero Beach's first public school and first motel, according to the Vero Beach Art Village organization.Over the years, parts of the neighborhood fell into disrepair. But where others saw aging properties and neglected alleyways, Power saw potential."It spoke to me, and I heard I was once great and now I have fallen into disrepair and not respected at all, and I said we're going to change that," Power told WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts during a tour of the neighborhood.Power has spent decades creating art and helping develop artistic communities, including an art center in Miami.Now, he's bringing that experience to Vero Beach, with an entire neighborhood as his canvas.Turning Edgewood's alleyways into works of artOne of Power's biggest ambitions is transforming 11 alleyways throughout Edgewood into colorful destinations filled with murals and public art."I'm taking the alleys which are the ugliest part of the neighborhood and turning them into mural opportunities where the alleys are going to be like unbelievable for people to come and visit," Power said."There's a lack of buildings but there's not a lack of fences."Power sees those fences, walls and underused spaces as opportunities to showcase local artists and create an outdoor art experience.But the effort goes beyond beautifying back streets.Special zoning allows artists to live and work in the villageThe city of Vero Beach has established Cultural Arts Village zoning districts designed to encourage artistic businesses while preserving Edgewood's historic residential character.According to the city and the Vero Beach Art Village organization, the zoning creates opportunities for art galleries, studios, live-work spaces and other businesses, depending on the property's classification and applicable approvals.The goal is to create a walkable neighborhood where historic homes can become studios and galleries, and artists can collaborate with their neighbors.“I’ve been working on a bunch of different paintings. And we have projects; there's a bunch of different projects we’ve been working on whether it’s for the city or for trying to save big blue, or our community garden, “ said Linwood Addison Fuller IV, an artist who moved to Edgewood for the focus on art. His wife is also an artist.“It’s so much better to be an artist in a community with other artists,” said sculptor Andrew Draminski. “I’m sitting here working and my neighbors are walking their dog down the alley and come on in and we have a cup of coffee or something like that.”The village's vision extends beyond traditional galleries. Organizers hope to create spaces for music, dance, poetry, photography, workshops and other community events.More galleries, studios and community spaces plannedAccording to the nonprofit Friends of the Vero Beach Art Village, the neighborhood's transformation is a grassroots effort involving artists, residents, businesses and volunteers.The organization highlights ongoing initiatives involving murals, public art, studios, galleries, streetscape improvements and community events.Power says additional galleries, studios, cafes and bed-and-breakfasts are also in the works.For him, the goal isn't simply to attract visitors. It's to create a community where artists can thrive together and residents can take pride in their neighborhood."If you want to eat great food, hear great music, see great things, meet great artists, this is the place," Power said.And beneath the sprawling branches of that century-old lychee tree, Power hopes the community he's helping cultivate will continue to grow.Where is the Vero Beach Art Village?The Vero Beach Art Village is located in the historic Edgewood neighborhood, just west of downtown Vero Beach.The neighborhood generally stretches between 14th and 20th avenues and 18th and 20th streets.The Friends of the Vero Beach Art Village nonprofit encourages residents and visitors to support the effort through volunteering, donations and participation in community art projects.Click here for more information about the village, its projects and opportunities to get involved.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

With more heavy rain possible this week, the City of Lake Worth Beach is taking steps to prepare as some residents continue recovering from last week's historic flooding.The city says it is closely monitoring weather conditions and working to maintain critical infrastructure in an effort to minimize additional flooding.WATCH REPORT BELOW:As part of those preparations, residents can pick up sandbags Tuesday from 12:30 p.m. and Wednesday from 10 a.m. at the Osborne Community Center, located at 1699 Wingfield St. The pickup is self-service, supplies are available while they last, and residents must provide proof of Lake Worth Beach residency.City crews are also working to address drainage concerns in areas vulnerable to flooding.Water Utilities crews are clearing storm drains along 18th Avenue South and in other flood-prone areas, including Bryant Park. Sewer collections crews are monitoring water levels along 7th Avenue North and South Lakeside Drive to help ensure the system is prepared for additional rainfall.During an interview with WPTV, Vice Mayor Mimi May said the city is working to get ahead of future storms."They are cleaning out the storm drains, they are making sure that there's no debris there, they are cleaning out the pump house that's in Bryant Park," May said.May said the city is also pursuing grants to strengthen its drainage infrastructure over the long term, while prioritizing maintenance and clearing existing systems in the immediate future.In the South Palm neighborhood, city leaders say crews recently removed nearly 23 yards of sediment from the sewer system, clearing an estimated 75% of a blockage.Although the neighborhood still experienced flooding, city leaders say removing the blockage weeks earlier helped prevent conditions from becoming significantly worse and helped keep raw sewage out of homes.Residents say they're still concerned about the possibility of more flooding.Natalie Samples, whose home experienced water intrusion during recent rainfall, said hearing more rain could be on the way immediately raised concerns about the damage already sustained."My first thought was, oh no, our floors are already ruined, and we've got to get in action and figure it out," Samples said.Another resident, Mario Spiteri, said his home is in a low-lying area and his garage was filled with water during the previous flooding."We don't want to get caught again," Spiteri said.In addition to sandbag distribution, Lake Worth Beach is offering storm recovery assistance for residents dealing with property damage.The city has announced complimentary debris pickup for storm-related flooding debris. Residents can contact Solid Waste at 561-533-7344 or solidwasteinfo@lakeworthbeachfl.gov to ask about scheduling a pickup.Residents who need repairs following flood damage can also contact the city's Building Division to request an expedited building permit at 561-586-1786 or BldgDiv@lakeworthbeachfl.gov.The Lake Worth Drainage District (LWDD) says its canals in southeastern Palm Beach County are prepared for a potentially heavy rainfall event.However, the district emphasizes that neighborhood drainage systems are also the responsibility of individual communities, homeowners associations and property managers.Residents are encouraged to safely clear debris from storm drains around their homes and report blocked internal drainage systems to the appropriate HOA or municipality.The district also reminds residents that emergency operable flood-control structures are not authorized to be opened at this time.As another round of rain approaches, officials are urging residents to avoid driving or walking through standing water and to use alternate routes when encountering flooded roadways.

Palm Beach County homeowners hoping for new financial help after this month's devastating flooding will have to wait a little longer.County commissioners voted 7-0 Tuesday to postpone consideration of a proposed $2 million Flood Disaster Assistance Program, choosing to spend more time working through questions about eligibility, insurance, contractors, temporary housing and how to stretch a limited amount of money among residents who need help.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The proposal is now expected to return to commissioners Dec. 1."We here at the Palm Beach County Commission wanna make sure that we get this right," Commissioner Bobby Powell Jr. told WPTV reporter Joel Lopez after the meeting. "Also, we need to hear from residents. 1 is when we'll have that meeting, and I would look forward to having residents come to that meeting. But also residents should call our offices, talk to us, and let's walk through this and work through it together."The proposed program comes roughly two weeks after extraordinary rainfall left neighborhoods underwater across Palm Beach County.In a previous meeting, county officials said parts of West Palm Beach received more than 22 inches of rain, causing roads to become waterways, leaving vehicles stranded and some residents unable to leave their neighborhoods. In Century Village near West Palm Beach, firefighters responded to more than seventy 911 calls in one night, with nearly 100 residents trapped in stranded vehicles as floodwaters rapidly rose. In Riviera Beach, the county's Swiftwater Response Team evacuated 71 people, conducted two medical rescues and evacuated nine pets.Powell, who represents District 7, was among those rescued during the flooding."Fire Rescue came to get me this morning, so I'm one of the people they had to rescue," Powell told commissioners during the meeting held earlier this month.Now, the county is trying to determine how to help residents recover.County staff proposed using $2 million from the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program to help income-qualified homeowners whose homesteaded properties suffered flood damage.SHIP is a state program funded through documentary stamp taxes that provides money to counties and qualifying municipalities for affordable housing programs.Under the proposal presented Tuesday, eligible homeowners could receive up to $50,000. The money could be used for uninsured structural damage that threatens health or safety, interim repairs to prevent additional damage, insurance deductibles and temporary relocation assistance."It's up to $50,000," Powell said. "Some homeowners may need less, some may need more, but this is a start. What we would like to do is analyze what the needs of the individuals who are requesting funding are so that we can better fulfill their needs."County officials said roughly 80 homes have reported damage so far, although officials noted that number depends on homeowners and municipalities reporting damage.They said they've been communicating with City of Riviera Beach officials who reported closer to 300 homes.The relatively small pool of money compared with the potential need quickly became a major part of Tuesday's discussion.If households received close to the proposed $50,000 maximum, commissioners noted the $2 million could help roughly 40 to 50 households. Some commissioners questioned whether that maximum should be lowered so the county could reach more families.They also raised concerns about whether assistance should simply be distributed on a first-come, first-qualified basis or whether the county should prioritize residents with the greatest need, including seniors and people whose homes are no longer habitable.Powell said what he has seen in some of the hardest-hit communities is difficult to describe."People have worked their entire lives to own a home. Or to get to where they have been in a safe and secure place, people have been put in a position where they no longer feel safe, comfortable, and protected," Powell said. "And able to thrive because their worldly possessions are sitting on the street corner because their house was damaged to an extent that they can no longer inhabit it by an event that they had not anticipated."Commissioners also spent considerable time questioning how the county would handle homeowners with insurance, people without flood insurance, contractor selection and residents who may also qualify for assistance offered by their cities.Temporary housing was another concern.The proposal included up to $10,000 of the $50,000 maximum for temporary relocation assistance for displaced residents for up to six months. Commissioners questioned whether those rules should be flexible enough to allow residents to stay with family members under certain circumstances, particularly given the cost and availability of short-term rentals in Palm Beach County.There were also questions about how the county should coordinate with municipalities such as Riviera Beach, which is exploring its own assistance for flood victims, while making sure residents are not reimbursed twice for the same expense."We have to work together. We have to resolve these issues together. It can be done," Powell said. "We need to work with the citizens, with the cities, the city of Riviera Beach, the city of West Palm Beach, and the county to come up with solutions that actually help people. There's no way around this."Powell acknowledged the frustration facing residents who have been seeking help since the flooding."This has been a problem since Nov. People have been reaching out asking for help, and now we're getting there; we're working on it, but we have to get it right," he said.County administrators originally hoped that, with commission approval Tuesday, applications could begin as soon as Wednesday. Instead, after more than an hour of discussion, commissioners agreed to give staff additional time to refine the proposal and bring it back Dec. 1.The county's efforts come as local leaders continue dealing with the aftermath of a flooding event that prompted Gov. Ron DeSantis to add Palm Beach County to Florida's state of emergency. The declaration provided additional authority and resources for response, recovery and mitigation efforts.For residents still waiting for help, Powell encouraged them to stay involved as county officials rework the program."We will get it right. We'll make sure we get assistance for people, and we'll keep working on it. Keep, keep showing up, keep knocking on doors. I know you're frustrated," Powell said. Do not stop."Powell also encouraged residents affected by the flooding to contact commissioners and participate when the proposal returns Dec. 1."It's our job and those who've been impacted to tell the stories and to show people so that we can make sure that you get the help that is needed and necessary," Powell said.With more rain possible, Powell urged residents to prepare for the possibility of additional flooding."Let's be proactive now we know the rain is coming. Let's do our best to be prepared," Powell said.He also called on government agencies to make sure drainage systems are ready."Let's make sure that every opportunity to drain water is working today so that we're not facing the same thing we saw last time."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Just weeks after historic flooding destroyed homes and displaced families in Jensen Beach, Martin County residents are bracing for another round of heavy rain — with up to 12 inches forecast over the next three days.For families still struggling to recover, the threat of more flooding comes as county commissioners work to determine what caused the initial disaster and how to help those who lost nearly everything.On Tuesday, flood victims packed a Martin County Commission meeting, pleading for financial assistance and answers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Along Cheri Drive in Jensen Beach, the signs of destruction remain. Dumpsters line driveways, damaged belongings sit outside and families are still trying to salvage what's left of their homes.Lisa French, her husband, Jeremy, and their two young sons are among those displaced after floodwaters rose as high as 3 feet inside some homes two weeks ago."It's like we're kind of stuck," French told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. French said her home had about 3 to 6 inches of flooding that sat inside for more than a week, causing mold to grow 3 to 4 feet up the walls. "So they, yeah, they tore the walls down in the house," said French. "They just chipped up the last bit of the tile, and it's empty." Now, with more rain approaching, French fears her family could face another disaster before recovering from the first."Of course, we're afraid because we all flooded in our houses," she said.New figures released by Martin County show at least 36 homes sustained damage, with an estimated $3 million in residential losses. Commissioners estimated another $14 million in damage to beaches, and at least $1 million in damage to roadways that now need repairs. For some residents, the destruction represents a lifetime of memories washed away."We've lost everything," one elderly Jensen Beach resident told commissioners. "We have 60 years of our life — kids, grandkids, everything. It's all gone."As residents demand answers about what went wrong, commissioners approved shifting $200,000 from the county's stormwater budget to investigate whether development and changes to local drainage systems contributed to the flooding.Commissioner Blake Capps called the investigation "a good starting point.""It may be that we need to augment the study beyond the $200,000 that we approve today," said Capps. Meanwhile, county crews are working around the clock to prepare for the next storm, lowering retention pond levels, deploying additional pumps and draining flooded properties."We have people 24 hours a day pumping that material down," Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said.Commissioners also approved financial assistance for eligible flood victims through the state's State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program.The assistance includes grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by liens on their properties.But there's a catch: The grants are reimbursement-based, meaning homeowners must first pay for eligible repairs before receiving the money.For families who lost everything, that presents another obstacle."We don't have $25,000," French said. "A lot of people don't have $25,000, so it's great, and we're appreciative, but I mean, our house is empty, and $25,000 is not going to do much for us." The other problem: the county currently has just $1 million in SHIP funding available, and commissioners warned the money could run out quickly, even with additional state funding promised."They haven't given us the amount yet, but they have assured us that we will be getting some disaster relief funds," said Human Services Director Michelle Miller Strict income limits could also disqualify some flood victims who cannot afford to rebuild on their own. The income cap for a family of one is $86,040. The cap for a family of two is $98,400. For a family of four, it's $122,880. When reporter Kate Hussey asked Capps what would happen to those families, he acknowledged the county needs to explore other options."There are going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where someone barely missed the limit, and we're going to need to take a look at what we can do for those folks," Capps said.For residents like French, the need is immediate."We just need somebody to step up," she said. "We need funding." With another round of heavy rain approaching, Martin County is distributing sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park to help residents protect their properties, with a limit of 25 per person. The County's Emergency Operations Center is scheduled to be staffed beginning Tuesday at 2 p.m., and the county is coordinating with the National Weather Service and Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM).Fire Rescue is also standing by with multiple high-water rescue trucks.Commissioners also said a Federal Emergency Management Agency representative is expected to visit Nov. 30 to assess the damage — a potential step toward securing federal disaster assistance.But for families still displaced and facing the possibility of more flooding, the uncertainty remains.

An 18-year-old driver has been arrested after a hit-and-run crash critically injured a 24-year-old woman on an electric scooter in Port St. Lucie, police said.WATCH: Update from Chief Leo NiemczykThe incident happened Monday morning near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace, Port St. Lucie police said.According to investigators, the victim was riding an electric scooter westbound on the sidewalk toward Southwest Rosser Boulevard. As the woman on the scooter entered the crosswalk, she was struck by the 18-year-old driver of a gray Chevrolet Tahoe making a left turn onto Southwest Feather Terrace.Police said the driver fled the scene and failed to stop to render aid to the woman.The Port St. Lucie Police Department's Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer and located the vehicle through its investigation. Lucie Public Schools will close all schools and district offices Wednesday, Nov. 18, as officials prepare for the potential for significant rainfall and localized flooding.The district announced the closure Tuesday, saying forecasts from the National Weather Service still have some uncertainty surrounding the exact timing, location and amount of rainfall.However, with the ground already saturated across the community, district leaders said they are taking a cautious approach in the interest of students, families and employees.All after-school activities, aftercare programs and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are also canceled.District officials said they will monitor rainfall, flooding and road closures throughout the day Wednesday. Football legend Joe Namath is bringing his popular Lucky Shuck restaurant to Jensen Beach as a massive waterfront development takes shape along the St. Rio Marine Village , a 30-acre mixed-use development in Martin County, broke ground Thursday, following more than five years of planning. The project will feature 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina, more than a half-mile of public riverwalk, and several waterfront dining and entertainment destinations. Among them is a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse , owned by Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica, along with a second, yet-to-be-named outdoor dining concept. See also: New 24/7 animal cruelty hotline launching across Florida "The Lucky Shuck has always been about good food, good people and being on the water," Namath said. "Rio Marine Village gives us a home right on the river, and I can't wait to see boats pulling up and families sitting down together." The development will also feature the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue, along with a public park, boardwalk, beach, and kayak and paddleboard rentals. Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions. Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028.

Pinewood Elementary School science teacher Richard Acosta has been named the 2026-27 Martin County Teacher of the Year, earning the opportunity to represent the county in the Florida Department of Education’s statewide Teacher of the Year competition.The Education Foundation of Martin County announced Acosta as the overall winner during its Teacher of the Year Award Celebration on Nov. 6 at the MIDFLORIDA Event Center in Port St. Lucie.Acosta was also named Elementary Teacher of the Year.“This is phenomenal,” Acosta said after the honor was revealed. “I feel incredibly invigorated and inspired to go to the next level and represent Martin County at the state competition.”Acosta was among three educators recognized with top honors.Miriam Hernández, an intensive reading teacher at Indiantown Middle School, was named Middle School Teacher of the Year.Marc Turull, who teaches International Baccalaureate physics and chemistry at South Fork High School, was named High School Teacher of the Year.Turull said the award also represents the people he works alongside.“It’s such an honor,” Turull said. “I teach physics, and I work with amazing people, so to represent them and be Teacher of the Year makes me so grateful.”Hernández described the recognition as both a privilege and an honor.During the celebration, the three teachers emphasized the importance of educators at every stage of a student's education.“The fact is that it takes all three of us for excellence in Martin County schools,” Acosta said. “We start with the foundation in elementary school. We move on to middle school intensive reading, and then we finish at the high school at South Fork. So we, we feel very blessed to be working together.”The Education Foundation said Acosta’s 35-year career in education can be traced partly to his own experience as a teenager.According to the Education Foundation of Martin County, at 16, Acosta was struggling with confidence and direction when he entered teacher John Lynskey’s American history class. According to the foundation, Lynskey’s storytelling and encouragement helped Acosta develop a love of learning.Acosta still keeps two history books Lynskey gave him.His path toward teaching became clearer when Acosta later tutored a younger student after school and watched the child's confidence and enthusiasm for learning grow, according to the foundation.Today, Acosta teaches science to students from prekindergarten through fifth grade at Pinewood Elementary.“I love what I do, and I love energizing the classroom and engaging them to the greatest possibility,” Acosta said.His lessons include hands-on investigations tied to the natural environment around Martin County. The Education Foundation said students have examined sea turtle skull models, shells and other materials connected to the Indian River Lagoon while studying how adaptations help turtles survive.Acosta also helped develop a “Birds of the Everglades” curriculum with environmental partners and has been involved with schoolwide science initiatives and family STEAM events.For Acosta, the recognition provides another opportunity beyond representing Martin County at the state level.“I feel very blessed to be in this position because I get to mentor other teachers from other schools,” Acosta said.Acosta also receives a one-year vehicle lease provided through Audi Stuart and Infiniti Stuart.“That is amazing and spectacular,” Acosta said. “I cannot wait to pick out a car on Saturday.”The celebration recognized 24 school-level Teachers of the Year who were selected by their peers. According to the Education Foundation, nominees submitted application portfolios and participated in interviews before a panel of judges.Felix A. Williams Elementary School also won the Spirit Award for its enthusiasm, interpretation of the event's theme, and props.The recognition comes as Martin County educators continue the everyday work behind the awards: helping children learn, building their confidence and creating connections that can influence students long after they leave the classroom.For Acosta, that circle is especially meaningful. A teacher once helped him see greater possibilities for his own future. Decades later, he is working to create those possibilities for another generation.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI.
