A historic Vero Beach neighborhood is getting a new life through art, as sculptor Ross Power leads an effort to transform Edgewood into a vibrant community of artists, galleries, studios and public gathering spaces.Known as the "Father of the Vero Beach Art Village," Power is helping turn a once-overlooked neighborhood into a destination for creativity, where artists can live, work and share their talents.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The transformation is already underway, with murals, public art and community projects taking shape. Power says more galleries, studios, cafes and bed-and-breakfasts are in the works, bringing new opportunities for artists, residents and visitors.A historic Vero Beach neighborhood becomes a canvasUnder the shade of a century-old lychee tree, Power reads from a poem dedicated to the tree as a dancer performs beneath its branches."A place where you and me can become we," Power said.For the longtime sculptor, the tree represents something bigger: a gathering place where art can bring people together.That vision is unfolding in Edgewood, a neighborhood established in 1916 that was once home to Vero Beach's first public school and first motel, according to the Vero Beach Art Village organization.Over the years, parts of the neighborhood fell into disrepair. But where others saw aging properties and neglected alleyways, Power saw potential."It spoke to me, and I heard I was once great and now I have fallen into disrepair and not respected at all, and I said we're going to change that," Power told WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts during a tour of the neighborhood.Power has spent decades creating art and helping develop artistic communities, including an art center in Miami.Now, he's bringing that experience to Vero Beach, with an entire neighborhood as his canvas.Turning Edgewood's alleyways into works of artOne of Power's biggest ambitions is transforming 11 alleyways throughout Edgewood into colorful destinations filled with murals and public art."I'm taking the alleys which are the ugliest part of the neighborhood and turning them into mural opportunities where the alleys are going to be like unbelievable for people to come and visit," Power said."There's a lack of buildings but there's not a lack of fences."Power sees those fences, walls and underused spaces as opportunities to showcase local artists and create an outdoor art experience.But the effort goes beyond beautifying back streets.Special zoning allows artists to live and work in the villageThe city of Vero Beach has established Cultural Arts Village zoning districts designed to encourage artistic businesses while preserving Edgewood's historic residential character.According to the city and the Vero Beach Art Village organization, the zoning creates opportunities for art galleries, studios, live-work spaces and other businesses, depending on the property's classification and applicable approvals.The goal is to create a walkable neighborhood where historic homes can become studios and galleries, and artists can collaborate with their neighbors.“I’ve been working on a bunch of different paintings. And we have projects; there's a bunch of different projects we’ve been working on whether it’s for the city or for trying to save big blue, or our community garden, “ said Linwood Addison Fuller IV, an artist who moved to Edgewood for the focus on art. His wife is also an artist.“It’s so much better to be an artist in a community with other artists,” said sculptor Andrew Draminski. “I’m sitting here working and my neighbors are walking their dog down the alley and come on in and we have a cup of coffee or something like that.”The village's vision extends beyond traditional galleries. Organizers hope to create spaces for music, dance, poetry, photography, workshops and other community events.More galleries, studios and community spaces plannedAccording to the nonprofit Friends of the Vero Beach Art Village, the neighborhood's transformation is a grassroots effort involving artists, residents, businesses and volunteers.The organization highlights ongoing initiatives involving murals, public art, studios, galleries, streetscape improvements and community events.Power says additional galleries, studios, cafes and bed-and-breakfasts are also in the works.For him, the goal isn't simply to attract visitors. It's to create a community where artists can thrive together and residents can take pride in their neighborhood."If you want to eat great food, hear great music, see great things, meet great artists, this is the place," Power said.And beneath the sprawling branches of that century-old lychee tree, Power hopes the community he's helping cultivate will continue to grow.Where is the Vero Beach Art Village?The Vero Beach Art Village is located in the historic Edgewood neighborhood, just west of downtown Vero Beach.The neighborhood generally stretches between 14th and 20th avenues and 18th and 20th streets.The Friends of the Vero Beach Art Village nonprofit encourages residents and visitors to support the effort through volunteering, donations and participation in community art projects.Click here for more information about the village, its projects and opportunities to get involved.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. If you've ever admired a perfectly golden Thanksgiving turkey and wondered how professional chefs make it look so good, Okeechobee Steakhouse co-owner Ralph Lewis has a surprisingly simple answer."It's butter."And not just a little butter.During a recent Thanksgiving cooking demonstration at Okeechobee Prime Meat Market, Lewis stood beside a giant inflatable stick of butter, worked from a table piled high with butter and seasonings, and even pulled a backup rubber stick of butter from his pocket.For Lewis, butter isn't simply an ingredient. It's the foundation of a great Thanksgiving turkey."Are you really supposed to have a budget with butter?" Lewis joked. "Those two words do not go together."According to Lewis, the biggest mistake many home cooks make is putting all of their butter on the outside of the bird.Instead, he recommends carefully separating the skin from the breast meat and creating pockets beneath the skin.Once those pockets are created, it's time to start adding butter.Lots of butter."You just want to keep working it in there," Lewis said. That's impossible, literally impossible, and that's a chef's code."As the turkey cooks, the butter melts beneath the skin, helping keep the meat moist while contributing to the rich color and flavor many Thanksgiving hosts are trying to achieve.After working butter beneath the skin, Lewis also coats the outside of the turkey before adding seasoning.One of the most useful tips Lewis shared involves seasoning the butter before it ever touches the bird.Start by taking butter out of the refrigerator and allowing it to soften to room temperature.Then combine the softened butter with herbs and seasonings such as:Kosher saltFreshly ground black pepperThymeRosemarySageMix everything together until it forms a seasoned compound butter.Then spread that butter beneath the skin and across the exterior of the turkey.By combining the herbs and seasoning directly into the butter, the flavors are distributed more evenly throughout the turkey as it cooks.Lewis says it's a simple step that can make a noticeable difference in flavor.Allow butter to come to room temperature.Mix the butter with kosher salt, black pepper, thyme, rosemary, sage or your favorite herbs.Gently separate the skin from the breast meat without tearing it.Spread seasoned butter beneath the skin and continue working it throughout the breast area.Coat the exterior of the turkey with additional butter.Add additional herbs and seasoning as desired.Place about a half-inch to one inch of water, chicken stock or turkey stock in the bottom of the pan.Cover the turkey with foil and roast at approximately 325 degrees.About 30 minutes before the turkey is done, remove the foil and increase the heat.Lewis says this final step helps create the deep golden-brown color that makes a Thanksgiving turkey look picture-perfect.Of course, Lewis' demonstration included a healthy helping of humor.At one point, while explaining his butter-heavy technique, he declared there is no such thing as too much butter.When told that Thanksgiving calories don't count, he quickly fired back:"What's calories?"And when asked whether anything should go inside the turkey cavity itself, his answer was immediate."Well, butter, of course."For families looking to spend less time in the kitchen and more time around the dinner table, Okeechobee Prime Meat Market is offering a variety of Thanksgiving meal packages featuring roasted or smoked turkeys, prime rib, beef tenderloin, traditional sides and holiday desserts.The market's Ultimate Holiday Family Feast serves 16 to 18 people and includes a Bell & Evans all-natural turkey, prime roasted beef tenderloin, stuffing, mashed potatoes, gravy, cranberry sauce and more.Pre-orders are available through Okeechobee Prime Meat Market in West Palm Beach.This article was drafted with the assistance of Microsoft Copilot using reporting, interview transcripts, and information gathered by WPTV journalist T.A. "I love the drivers, the teachers, the staff, the employees. I love everybody here, my friends."When asked what she enjoys most about being on the team, Sheila quickly listed some of the people who have made an impact on her."I like about the cheerleaders, cheer squad, even Michelle, Miss Britney, and everybody," she said.The cheer team will perform at schools and community events throughout Palm Beach County, giving participants a chance to be visible, celebrated and involved.Scott said the program is about more than cheering. Italian food, live music and family traditions return to Abacoa Town Center this weekend as the Galbani Feast of Little Italy celebrates its 25th anniversary Nov. 6-8 with three days of festivities and free admission, according to organizers.The festival runs from 4 to 10 p.m. Sunday.This year's milestone celebration includes Italian food, cooking demonstrations, live entertainment, family activities and an unusual attempt to make festival history using string cheese.Food is at the heart of the weekend.Festival organizers say guests can expect Italian-American favorites including pasta, sausage and peppers, Neapolitan pizza, zeppole, cannoli and gelato.The Galbani Cooking Stage will feature demonstrations throughout the weekend, giving festivalgoers a chance to watch chefs prepare dishes and pick up cooking tips.The published lineup includes Anthony Acampa, Sicilian Oven Chef Andrew, Galbani Chef Marco Sciortino (with special guest Joe Gannascoli from The Sopranos), Cooking with Vinny, Nina's Fresh Bakery and Michelin-starred chef Joe Isidori. Voga wine seminars are also scheduled during the weekend.Saturday brings one of the festival's most unusual attractions.At 4 p.m., organizers are inviting festivalgoers to participate in an event billed as “Let's Make Italian Festival History!” The goal is to bring people together to simultaneously string string cheese.The public is encouraged to participate, turning a familiar snack into one of the quirkiest moments of the festival's 25th anniversary.The 25th anniversary celebration also brings three days of live entertainment to Abacoa.Friday's schedule includes Angelo Venuto before The Studio 54 Band takes the main stage at 8 p.m.Saturday's lineup includes Daniela Martino at 3 p.m., with Frank Stallone headlining at 8 p.m.Sunday's performers include James Valenti and Franco Corso. Boca Helping Hands is asking the community to help provide Thanksgiving meals for more than 4,000 Palm Beach County families through its annual Thanksgiving Box Brigade.The nonprofit is asking donors to contribute $29.72, the cost of a Thanksgiving box that helps provide families facing food insecurity with the ingredients for a holiday meal.WATCH REPORT BELOW: For families already stretching household budgets, Boca Helping Hands CEO Dr. Andrew Hagen said the added cost of Thanksgiving can make the holiday particularly difficult."You know this has been a tough year for a lot of people economically, and we want to make sure they have a good Thanksgiving," Hagen said.Boca Helping Hands plans to distribute turkeys and Thanksgiving meal boxes to current Pantry Bag Program clients Nov. 21 and 22 at five drive-thru locations in East Boca Raton, West Boca Raton, Delray Beach, Boynton Beach and Lake Worth Beach.Volunteers pack thousands of Thanksgiving boxesPreparing thousands of Thanksgiving meals requires plenty of hands.Volunteers gathered at the Boca Helping Hands food center in Boca Raton to pack the boxes, including a group from Vivmark Residential.Hagen credited the volunteers and community supporters with making the effort possible."We're going to be able to provide at least 4,000 families with Thanksgiving meals, and that's because of the people here today, thanks to you and thanks to all the people that support Boca Helping Hands," Hagen said.To demonstrate the work that goes into the effort, volunteers from Vivmark Residential and The Boca Raton (who donated 100 turkeys) turned packing into a friendly competition. Each team packed 12 boxes, ending the challenge in a tie.Turning a Thanksgiving box into dinnerThe ingredients inside the boxes are intended to give families the foundation for preparing their own Thanksgiving meals at home.Chef Andrew "Andy" Roenbeck, vice president of culinary operations and group executive chef at The Boca Raton, demonstrated how some additional ingredients families may already have can add new flavors to the meal.Roenbeck added apples to stuffing and Florida orange to cranberry sauce. He topped pumpkin pie with meringue and gave it a toasted finish.And when it came to the stuffing, he offered a simple Thanksgiving philosophy."Everything's better with butter," Roenbeck said.The demonstration offered a look at what the ingredients packed by volunteers can ultimately become: a Thanksgiving meal served around a family’s table.How to help Boca Helping HandsCommunity members can support the Thanksgiving Box Brigade by donating the $29.72 cost of a box through Boca Helping Hands.The campaign comes as the nonprofit prepares to serve more than 4,000 families across Palm Beach County for Thanksgiving, turning individual donations and hours of volunteer work into meals families can prepare and share at home.Click here for more information about the Thanksgiving Box Brigade.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.What do you want me to Shine A Light on? What are you most proud of where you live? Veterans of all eras and residents of all ages packed Veterans Memorial Park in Port St. Lucie on Wednesday for the annual Veterans Day ceremony.WPTV anchor and Navy veteran Mike Trim connected with fellow veterans about the significance of the day.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Vietnam veteran Michael Greene wore a newly decorated vest commemorating his Army service "It's all like my whole history. I started in transportation. I think it's very important. I enlisted and was not supposed to go but ended up over there," Greene told Trim.Wayne Thomas, another Vietnam War veteran in attendance, told Trim he felt this day now properly honors their service, which was not previously recognized."It's good to get the recognition that we didn't get," Thomas said.The Port St. Lucie High School Junior ROTC attended the ceremony in full force while crowds of all ages looked on.That included a member of the greatest generation: 98-year-old World War II veteran Robert Vogel."I'm one of the few left. I would really encourage anyone to come to these events because they're really important to support the veterans," Vogel told Trim.Those veterans heard keynote speaker, Retired Air Force Master Sgt. Vincent Lavelle Jr.A special touch from the Port St. Lucie community band featured songs from each branch of service.That prompted service members in attendance to stand for their respective branch song.There was also a special flyover by the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office helicopter.

Just weeks after historic flooding destroyed homes and displaced families in Jensen Beach, Martin County residents are bracing for another round of heavy rain — with up to 12 inches forecast over the next three days.For families still struggling to recover, the threat of more flooding comes as county commissioners work to determine what caused the initial disaster and how to help those who lost nearly everything.On Tuesday, flood victims packed a Martin County Commission meeting, pleading for financial assistance and answers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Along Cheri Drive in Jensen Beach, the signs of destruction remain. Dumpsters line driveways, damaged belongings sit outside and families are still trying to salvage what's left of their homes.Lisa French, her husband, Jeremy, and their two young sons are among those displaced after floodwaters rose as high as 3 feet inside some homes two weeks ago."It's like we're kind of stuck," French told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. French said her home had about 3 to 6 inches of flooding that sat inside for more than a week, causing mold to grow 3 to 4 feet up the walls. "So they, yeah, they tore the walls down in the house," said French. "They just chipped up the last bit of the tile, and it's empty." Now, with more rain approaching, French fears her family could face another disaster before recovering from the first."Of course, we're afraid because we all flooded in our houses," she said.New figures released by Martin County show at least 36 homes sustained damage, with an estimated $3 million in residential losses. Commissioners estimated another $14 million in damage to beaches, and at least $1 million in damage to roadways that now need repairs. For some residents, the destruction represents a lifetime of memories washed away."We've lost everything," one elderly Jensen Beach resident told commissioners. "We have 60 years of our life — kids, grandkids, everything. It's all gone."As residents demand answers about what went wrong, commissioners approved shifting $200,000 from the county's stormwater budget to investigate whether development and changes to local drainage systems contributed to the flooding.Commissioner Blake Capps called the investigation "a good starting point.""It may be that we need to augment the study beyond the $200,000 that we approve today," said Capps. Meanwhile, county crews are working around the clock to prepare for the next storm, lowering retention pond levels, deploying additional pumps and draining flooded properties."We have people 24 hours a day pumping that material down," Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said.Commissioners also approved financial assistance for eligible flood victims through the state's State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program.The assistance includes grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by liens on their properties.But there's a catch: The grants are reimbursement-based, meaning homeowners must first pay for eligible repairs before receiving the money.For families who lost everything, that presents another obstacle."We don't have $25,000," French said. "A lot of people don't have $25,000, so it's great, and we're appreciative, but I mean, our house is empty, and $25,000 is not going to do much for us." The other problem: the county currently has just $1 million in SHIP funding available, and commissioners warned the money could run out quickly, even with additional state funding promised."They haven't given us the amount yet, but they have assured us that we will be getting some disaster relief funds," said Human Services Director Michelle Miller Strict income limits could also disqualify some flood victims who cannot afford to rebuild on their own. The income cap for a family of one is $86,040. The cap for a family of two is $98,400. For a family of four, it's $122,880. When reporter Kate Hussey asked Capps what would happen to those families, he acknowledged the county needs to explore other options."There are going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where someone barely missed the limit, and we're going to need to take a look at what we can do for those folks," Capps said.For residents like French, the need is immediate."We just need somebody to step up," she said. "We need funding." With another round of heavy rain approaching, Martin County is distributing sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park to help residents protect their properties, with a limit of 25 per person. The County's Emergency Operations Center is scheduled to be staffed beginning Tuesday at 2 p.m., and the county is coordinating with the National Weather Service and Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM).Fire Rescue is also standing by with multiple high-water rescue trucks.Commissioners also said a Federal Emergency Management Agency representative is expected to visit Nov. 30 to assess the damage — a potential step toward securing federal disaster assistance.But for families still displaced and facing the possibility of more flooding, the uncertainty remains.

Martin County families still recovering from this month’s flooding are bracing for more rain, and on Tuesday, many of them asked county commissioners not to wait on federal help before opening an emergency shelter. Speaker after speaker told commissioners during public comment that water was already back in their streets. Some said their homes took on water earlier this month. Their main request was a public shelter, open before the next round of rain, for both unhoused residents and families who lost their homes in the flooding. Commissioners are discussing funding options at both the local and federal level. Florida has asked President Donald Trump for a major disaster declaration for the flooding, and as of Tuesday, it had not been signed. Once a disaster receives a federal declaration, FEMA must cover 75 percent of state and local response and recovery costs, according to the Florida Policy Institute. Without one, counties pay those costs on their own. Several speakers argued the county does not need to wait for that approval to act. Commissioner, you do not need FEMA’s blessing to open a school. Neighboring counties didn’t wait. Churches didn’t wait, one speaker said. Yamila Rollan Escalona, founder and executive director of Yaya Por Vida, a grassroots harm reduction organization, said she emailed her comments Tuesday morning as water rose in her neighborhood again, then came to speak in person. She said her group has been asking commissioners for emergency shelter for most of the year. See also: Palm Beach County braces for more flooding as cities offer sandbags, prepare for storm Please give us emergency shelter now. It’s no longer about just individuals that are unhoused. It’s also about individuals that just became unhoused because of this tragedy, Rollan Escalona told CBS12 News after the meeting. Rollan Escalona said unhoused residents have nowhere to go, pointing to a 2024 state law that bans sleeping on public property. She said some people are still staying in campsites surrounded by standing water, and some residents have not been accounted for. With drains and the ground already saturated, she said there is no time to wait. She also warned the damage won’t end when the water goes down. Rollan Escalona said mental health services on the Treasure Coast are already hard to access, and she worries the stress and hopelessness of losing everything could lead to more overdoses and people returning to substance use. Other speakers looked further ahead, linking the flooding to development in the county, including a proposed hyperscale data center. They asked commissioners to consider runoff and drainage before approving large projects. Take the 30,000-foot view the next time you look at a large project. How does it affect your neighbors? Martin County Emergency Management Director Sally Waite previously told commissioners the flooding affected 77 homes. Residents whose homes were damaged can report it and fill out a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page. Ahead of the rain, Martin County is handing out sand and sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park, 8303 SW Lost River Road. Distribution runs from noon to 6 p.m. Each household can take up to 25 sandbags, and residents will be asked for their name and address. The county asks residents to check its map for the exact pickup spot inside the park. CBS12 News will update this story with what commissioners decide on funding and a possible shelter.

Martin County officials announced their plans to support flood victims as they begin the long road to recovery. County commissioners fielded hours of public comment at their meeting Tuesday. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 The county has set up a sandbag distribution site at Halpatiokee Regional Park where folks can fill up to 25 sandbags per household. That is just one part of what they’re doing to prepare for more storms and help residents. “The county needs to help us. Somebody needs to come forward. There's got to be an emergency fund. I can't understand how Martin County, one of the richest counties in Florida, does not have one,” Mary Berner, who lost her home on Hyline Drive in the flood, said. One by one, residents stepped to the podium at the meeting airing their frustrations at the flood disaster response. “We sat there for eight days and didn't have any response until we had a, you know, a meeting and made several phone calls to our commissioner and got no response from her. So, it's hard to not be heard,” Berner said. Commissioners made sure those pleas were heard Tuesday. They approved an increase of an up to $25,000 in grant funding for each eligible household from the county’s SHIP Disaster Assistance fund. Eligibility is determined by household income based on HUD guidelines. “These funds come through the state through something called the Sadowski funds. These funds are captured for each county when there's a real estate transaction, and then the state delivers to each county a certain amount each year to allocate for not only disaster, but things like rehabilitation of your home,” Michelle Miller, Martin County Human Services director, said. The county currently has $900,000 in that fund. “There are certain eligibility uses for that disaster funding, which, again, are expenses to weatherproof your house, rental assistance ... also, emergency hotel vouchers,” Miller said. As far as preps go, Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton told commissioners that right now, crews are pumping several lakes and ponds to create more space for any excess water to go. He said they’re especially focusing on the Hyline Drive area where Berner’s home is and was destroyed. “There's no way to rebuild if you have nothing. And I mean, literally nothing is left. And then, of course, long-term goals, they need to figure out this problem; they need to stop developing in wetlands,” Berner said. To apply for the SHIP emergency funding, applicants should go to the county’s human services office or call 772-320-3169. As for the sandbags, residents can grab them Wednesday from 7 a.m. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

Strong winds and high surf are creating dangerous conditions along the Treasure Coast and Palm Beaches, with red flag warnings and a high risk of rip currents keeping most beachgoers out of the water. At Stuart Beach, the wind is whipping through the area, churning up rough water conditions. The beach is nearly empty, with no one in the water and only a few people on the sand. "Take advantage of this; it may not be great weather, but there's not a lot of people. So, you got quiet time to yourself. It's beautiful," said Jon Ciffolillo, a beachgoer. Despite the roaring wind, some are still venturing out to enjoy the morning before another round of heavy rain is expected to move through the area. "It's a beautiful day out here. The wind and the surf is just a different view of nature's beauty," said Frank Harvey, who was walking on the beach with his wife, Joan. Joan Harvey added, "A lot of time in your condo is not always ideal. So, you got to take it when it's not raining." Beachgoers are being urged to take caution, as conditions in the water remain dangerous. A high surf advisory is in effect along the Palm Beaches and Treasure Coast, along with a high risk for rip currents. Red flag warnings are also in place along Martin County's beaches, signaling that even experienced swimmers can be pulled away from shore. Martin County Ocean Rescue advises beachgoers to check with lifeguards about water conditions and to swim in guarded areas when conditions improve. The high surf advisory and high risk for rip currents are expected to last through Thursday. You can check the latest beach conditions across Martin County on their Safe Beach Day website. As the threat of another round of November rain and flooding takes aim at Florida's east coast, many local governments are once again preparing for what may be ahead. "I think everybody is well aware now that this storm drain system was not designed for the flooding we're getting nowadays," St. Lucie County spokesman Erick Gill said.WATCH REPORT BELOW: He said crews are being deployed across the county as they were two weeks ago. "There were probably 50 to 100 staff members out there, including crews in public works, out in the field working during the storm. That's unbudgeted overtime," Gill said. This week, the county offered free sand, donated by Dickerson Infrastructure and Stewart Materials, for residents to bag. Other services cost money, and Gill said budgeting is already on the minds of county leaders now that the Amendment 3 tax cuts are coming. What is uncertain is how the loss of revenue will affect things like storm preparation and response. "We still don't know what the total impacts will be for, you know, with Amendment 3 with the additional homestead exemption," Gill said. "We're looking at the early estimates in this next upcoming fiscal year to be about a $60 million shortfall and then about $120 million once the exemption goes up."

A 24-year-old woman who was critically injured in a hit-and-run crash while riding an electric scooter in Port St. Lucie has died, according to police. The crash happened around 5:10 a.m. 16 near the intersection of Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace, according to the Port St. Officers said the victim was struck by a vehicle whose driver fled the scene without stopping to provide aid or contact law enforcement. Investigators with the department's Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit later identified the vehicle involved as a gray Chevrolet Tahoe and located it at a residence in Port St. Police identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer, 18. According to investigators, Sanchez-Chasmer had been participating in a game of "ding dong ditch" with friends shortly before the crash. Police said he struck the scooter rider while leaving a residence where the group had been carrying out the prank and then left the scene. Sanchez-Chasmer was arrested and charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, a second-degree felony under Florida law. The victim died at approximately 9:23 p.m. Following her death, the Port St. Lucie Police Department said it expects the State Attorney's Office to pursue enhanced and/or additional charges as the investigation continues. In a news release issued Wednesday morning, police extended condolences to the victim's family and loved ones, describing the death as a tragic loss for the community Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates

Lucie County residents are preparing for heavy rainfall this week, with officials offering free self-serve sandbag stations and working to clear drainage systems to address potential flooding. Dreamland Park in Fort Pierce, residents were seen filling sandbags to protect their homes. Resident Lisa Powell is concerned. "My ditches are full from the last storm, they haven't gone down, so this could be very bad. The water is just still standing there, up to the yard." Another resident shared their concerns, saying, "My crawlspace got a foot of water in there, so trying to get all these bags to try and cover up the opening, you know." Public works crews in St. Lucie County are actively checking and clearing swales and drainage systems as the area braces for more severe weather. Recent flooding left parts of the county submerged, with residents in the Creekside development trapped inside, some using kayaks to navigate flooded streets while others waded through the water. Fredrick Reeves, a resident whose home was previously flooded, is preparing for the upcoming rain by using sandbags and mulch to block water from entering his house. "It was pretty bad, and the house itself, once it started coming in, I thought maybe we would be alright. I threw down all my clothes trying to soak it up, but that didn't do anything. The next thing you knew, it was in the house," Reeves said. He described the situation as "overwhelming." The City of Fort Pierce is offering free self-serve sandbag stations at Martin Luther King Jr. Dreamland Park and Jaycee Park. Residents are advised to bring their own bags and shovels. Both parks are open daily from dawn to dusk. Lucie County has also set up self-service sandbag distribution points at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds West Parking Lot and Lawnwood Stadium Parking Lot, thanks to donations of sand from Dickerson Infrastructure and Stewart Materials. Residents must bring their own supplies and fill their own bags. For updates about the precautions residents should take, please visit St. Lucie County’s emergency management portal at: www.readystlucie.org. For more information, residents can contact the Public Works Department or visit the county’s emergency management portal. A 24-year-old woman riding her e-scooter to work was critically injured in a hit-and-run early Monday morning near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace in Port St. Body camera footage shows police responding to the scene, where the woman was found unconscious in the road. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said the driver left the scene without stopping to render aid or contact law enforcement. Detectives identified the vehicle and traced it back to 18-year-old Tristan Sanchez Chasmer. According to Niemczyk, Chasmer and two passengers had just ding-dong ditched a home about a mile from the crash site. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 "He was trying to get away from playing a prank," Niemczyk said. "So I think it would be reasonable to conclude that he was not driving with all due care that he normally would." Niemczyk said the two passengers exited the truck shortly after the crash, but none of them called 911. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app. "They're aware that they hit something. I'll say that," Niemczyk said. A witness called 911 and helped the victim, who was airlifted to the hospital. She remains in critical condition. "We're deeply concerned for her recovery and our thoughts are with her loved ones," Niemczyk said. Chasmer was arrested on one count of fleeing the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury and is being held on a $5,000 bond. The two passengers are not facing charges.

Families across the Treasure Coast are watching the forecast closely after historic flooding overwhelmed parts of Port St. Just as many neighborhoods are drying out, forecasters are warning another 4 to 6 inches of rain could fall over the next few days, raising concerns about renewed flooding in areas still recovering from the record rainfall. The flooding two weeks ago left cars stranded, some families trapped in their homes and others wading through deep water. "It was horrible," said Port St. Lucie resident Crisostomo Santiago Perez. "Water was on top of the cars almost, covering hoods." Among those caught off guard was freshman Noah Julian. 2, Noah stepped off his school bus to find his neighborhood along Coleman Avenue flooded. A video recorded by neighbor Martina Elieson quickly spread on social media, showing the teenager swimming through floodwaters just to reach his driveway. "When I see the video, I'm like, what?" said Noah's father, Romeo Julian. We got alligators here, snakes, sharp objects could have cut him up. A thousand things could've happened to him." With another round of heavy rain in the forecast, residents say they aren't taking any chances." "Today I'm going to get stuff before flood comes," Perez said. See also: From banks to flights, outages leave south Floridians frustrated St. Lucie Public Schools is also preparing ahead of the storm. The district announced a two-hour early release Tuesday in an effort to avoid a repeat of the flooding issues that affected students taking the bus home earlier this month. "But why it always takes one thing to make them wake up." Meanwhile, county crews have been inspecting and clearing canals and drainage systems ahead of the expected rainfall. Officials warn that because the ground is still saturated from recent storms, it will take far less rain than usual to cause flooding in neighborhoods, streets and other low-lying areas. Residents are encouraged to monitor local forecasts and be prepared for changing conditions as the rain moves into the area.

hero.headline: 24-year-old scooter rider dies after Port St. Lucie hit-and-run crash
hero.body:
A 24-year-old woman died Tuesday night from injuries she suffered when a vehicle struck her electric scooter in a hit-and-run crash in Port St. Lucie, police said Wednesday. The woman died at approximately 9:23 p.m. Tuesday, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.

The crash happened around 5:10 a.m. Monday near the intersection of Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Investigators allege the driver left the scene without stopping to help the woman or notify law enforcement. The department's Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit later identified the vehicle as a gray Chevrolet Tahoe and located it at a Port St. Lucie home, police said.

Investigators identified the alleged driver as 18-year-old Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer. He was arrested and charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, a second-degree felony, according to police. Investigators learned Sanchez-Chasmer had been playing “ding dong ditch” with friends shortly before the crash, police said. According to the department, the group was leaving a home where they had been participating in the prank when the vehicle struck the woman.

Following the woman's death, police said they anticipate the State Attorney's Office will pursue enhanced or additional charges as appropriate, based on the circumstances and the outcome of the investigation.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County schools, district offices closed Wednesday over flooding concerns
hero.body:
All St. Lucie County public schools and district offices are closed Wednesday over concerns about heavy rain and localized flooding. The district also canceled all aftercare programs, after-school activities and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday. It plans to announce Wednesday evening whether schools will reopen Thursday.

The district said forecasts show the potential for significant rainfall on already saturated ground. It described the closure as a cautious choice for students, families and employees. Officials are monitoring rainfall, flooding, road closures and access to schools, bus stops and transportation routes. Updates about school operations will be posted on the district’s website and social media channels.

The closures come two weeks after flooding left roads underwater and damaged homes. Across the Treasure Coast, residents are filling sandbags, stocking up on groceries and preparing to stay home if roads flood again.

St. Lucie County has set up self-service sand distribution sites at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds in Fort Pierce and the Lawnwood Stadium parking lot. Residents must bring their own bags and shovels, then fill the bags themselves. Sand is available while supplies last. On Tuesday, the two truckloads at Lawnwood Stadium were nearly gone.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie scooter rider dies after hit-and-run; charges could be upgraded
cards.teaser: The 24-year-old woman was critically injured Monday near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Police expect prosecutors to pursue enhanced or additional charges against the driver.
cards.body:
A 24-year-old woman critically injured while riding an electric scooter in a hit-and-run crash Monday morning in Port St. Lucie has died, police said. The driver faces a charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, and police now expect prosecutors to pursue enhanced or additional charges.

The crash happened around 5:10 a.m. near the intersection of Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Officers said the driver struck the woman and fled without stopping to provide aid or contact law enforcement.

Police identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer, 18. Investigators said he had been participating in a game of “ding dong ditch” with friends shortly before the crash. According to police, he struck the scooter rider while leaving a residence where the group had been carrying out the prank, then left the scene.

Investigators with the department’s Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit identified the vehicle involved as a gray Chevrolet Tahoe and located it at a residence. Sanchez-Chasmer was arrested and charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, a second-degree felony under Florida law.

Following the woman’s death, the Port St. Lucie Police Department said it expects the State Attorney’s Office to pursue enhanced or additional charges as the investigation continues. In a news release Wednesday morning, police extended condolences to the woman’s family and loved ones.

hero.headline: Florida animal cruelty hotline draws more than 30 calls, leads to Bay County dog rescue
hero.body:
Florida’s new statewide hotline for reporting suspected animal abuse has received more than 30 calls and led to the rescue of an abandoned and neglected dog in Bay County, according to Big Dog Ranch Rescue CEO and founder Lauree Simmons.

Simmons said the Florida Statewide Animal Cruelty Hotline went live Monday. Big Dog Ranch Rescue, located in Loxahatchee Groves, operates the state-funded hotline.

Treasure Coast residents and people throughout Florida can report suspected abuse anonymously by calling 844-4-SOSPET (844-476-7738). The hotline is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, and accepts reports of cruelty, abandonment and dog fighting.

Reports are turned over to law enforcement, animal control or a government agency for possible investigation. Simmons urged people who see animals being neglected or starved to call and report it.

hero.headline: Indian River County schools to stay open Wednesday despite heavy-rain concerns
hero.body:
The School District of Indian River County will keep schools open on a regular schedule Wednesday, Nov. 18, for students and employees despite concerns about heavy rainfall. Extended Day and extracurricular activities will also operate, and absences will not be excused solely because of the weather.

The district announced its decision Tuesday afternoon. “Families are encouraged to make the best decision for their circumstances,” a district spokesperson said. Weather-related absences will follow standard attendance procedures.

Elsewhere on the Treasure Coast, St. Lucie County Public Schools announced Tuesday that schools would close to students and employees Wednesday. All afterschool activities, after-care programs and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday were canceled. A district spokesperson cited National Weather Service forecasts indicating the potential for significant rainfall and localized flooding, along with already saturated conditions. District officials will monitor rainfall, flooding, road closures and access to schools, bus stops and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision about reopening Thursday will be announced Wednesday evening, with updates on the district’s website and social media platforms.

John Carroll High School in Fort Pierce also announced a Wednesday closure because of the potential for heavy rainfall and flooding throughout the region. All school-sponsored activities, including athletics, practices, extracurricular programs and other events, were canceled. The private school anticipates resuming normal operations Thursday, Nov. 19, pending weather and road conditions. Administrators will continue monitoring forecasts and communicating with local authorities. All after-school programs and Clubhouse locations operated by Boys Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County will also be closed Wednesday.

The Martin County School District will keep schools and Extended Day open Wednesday, but all other after-school activities, athletic practices and events are canceled. Martin County officials will monitor weather conditions. All Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County locations are scheduled to reopen Wednesday and resume normal operating hours.

hero.headline: Martin County approves $200,000 flood investigation as more rain threatens Jensen Beach
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners approved shifting $200,000 from the county’s stormwater budget Tuesday to investigate whether development and drainage changes contributed to flooding in Jensen Beach, where damaged neighborhoods face another heavy rain forecast. Up to 12 inches of rain is forecast over three days as families continue recovering from flooding two weeks ago. Commissioner Blake Capps called the investigation “a good starting point” and said the county may need to expand the study beyond the initial $200,000.

County figures show at least 36 homes sustained damage, with estimated residential losses of $3 million. Commissioners estimated another $14 million in beach damage and at least $1 million in roadway damage. Along Cheri Drive, dumpsters line driveways and damaged belongings sit outside homes. Lisa French, her husband, Jeremy, and their two young sons are among those displaced. French said 3 to 6 inches of water remained inside her home for more than a week, causing mold to grow 3 to 4 feet up the walls.

Commissioners also approved recovery assistance through the state’s State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program, including grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by property liens. The grants reimburse eligible repairs, requiring homeowners to pay first. “We don't have $25,000,” French said. The income caps are $86,040 for a one-person household, $98,400 for two people and $122,880 for four. Capps said commissioners would need to examine options for residents who narrowly exceed those limits.

The county currently has $1 million in SHIP funding available, and commissioners warned it could run out quickly. Human Services Director Michelle Miller said the state has assured the county it will receive disaster relief funds. Residents packed Tuesday’s commission meeting seeking financial help and answers about the flooding. French said her home’s walls had been torn down and the last of its tile removed. “We just need somebody to step up,” she said. “We need funding.”

County crews are working around the clock to lower retention pond levels, deploy additional pumps and drain flooded properties. Martin County is distributing sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park, with a limit of 25 per person, and coordinating with the National Weather Service and Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM). Fire Rescue is standing by with multiple high-water rescue trucks. Commissioners said a Federal Emergency Management Agency representative is expected to visit Nov. 30 to assess damage, a potential step toward federal disaster assistance.

cards.headline: Martin County schools, Extended Day open Wednesday; other activities canceled
cards.teaser: The Martin County School District will keep schools and Extended Day open Wednesday while canceling all other after-school activities, athletic practices and events amid heavy-rain concerns.
cards.body:
The Martin County School District will keep schools and Extended Day open to students Wednesday, Nov. 18, but has canceled all other after-school activities, athletic practices and events because of anticipated rainfall. Martin County officials will monitor weather conditions. All Boys Girls Clubs of Martin County locations also will reopen Wednesday and resume normal operating hours. The announcements come as schools and after-school programs across the Treasure Coast set different schedules in response to forecasts of heavy rainfall and concerns about flooding.

St. Lucie County Public Schools will be closed to students and employees Wednesday, a district spokesperson announced Tuesday, Nov. 17. All afterschool activities, after-care programs and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are canceled. The spokesperson cited National Weather Service forecasts indicating the potential for significant rainfall and localized flooding, along with already saturated conditions. “While there remains some uncertainty regarding the exact timing, location, and amount of rainfall,” the spokesperson said, the district determined a cautious approach was best for students, families and employees. Officials will monitor rainfall, flooding, road closures and access to schools, bus stops and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision about reopening Thursday will be announced Wednesday evening, with updates posted on the district’s website and social media platforms.

John Carroll High School in Fort Pierce also will close Wednesday because of the potential for heavy rainfall and flooding throughout the region. The private school said the decision followed Tuesday’s early dismissal and a review of forecasts and local flooding conditions. All school-sponsored activities Wednesday, including athletics, practices, extracurricular programs and other events, are canceled. The school anticipates resuming normal operations Thursday, Nov. 19, pending weather and road conditions. Administrators will monitor forecasts and communicate with local authorities. All Boys Girls Clubs of St. Lucie County after-school programs and Clubhouse locations also will be closed Wednesday.

The School District of Indian River County will follow a regular schedule Wednesday for students and employees, including Extended Day and extracurricular activities. In its Tuesday afternoon announcement, the district said teams had found no standing water affecting safe routes to bus stops. Families were encouraged to make the best decision for their circumstances. The district said weather-related absences would follow standard attendance procedures and would not be excused solely because of weather.

cards.headline: Martin County residents press commissioners for emergency shelter before more rain
cards.teaser: Residents urged commissioners Tuesday to open a public shelter for unhoused people and families displaced by flooding. Commissioners are discussing local and federal funding options.
cards.body:
Martin County residents urged county commissioners Tuesday to open an emergency shelter before more rain arrives, asking them to act rather than wait for federal help. Speakers sought a public shelter for both unhoused residents and families who lost their homes in this month’s flooding.

During public comment, residents said water was already returning to their streets. Some said their homes had flooded earlier this month. Yamila Rollan Escalona, founder and executive director of Yaya Por Vida, a grassroots harm reduction organization, said she emailed her comments Tuesday morning as water rose again in her neighborhood. She then attended the meeting to speak. She said her organization has been asking commissioners for emergency shelter for most of the year.

Rollan Escalona said some unhoused residents were still staying in campsites surrounded by standing water. She pointed to a 2024 state law banning sleeping on public property and urged commissioners to provide shelter for people displaced by the flooding as well as those already unhoused. With drains and the ground saturated, she said the need was urgent. She also raised concerns about the longer-term effects of losing homes and belongings, saying mental health services on the Treasure Coast are already hard to access. She warned that stress and hopelessness could contribute to overdoses and a return to substance use.

Commissioners are discussing local and federal funding options. Florida has asked President Donald Trump for a major disaster declaration for the flooding. According to the Florida Policy Institute, a federal disaster declaration requires FEMA to cover 75 percent of the response and recovery costs incurred by state and local governments. Several speakers urged commissioners to open a shelter before federal approval, arguing that the county could act on its own.

Martin County Emergency Management Director Sally Waite previously told commissioners that flooding affected 77 homes. Residents with damaged homes can report damage and complete a needs survey on the county’s flood recovery page. The county is distributing sand and sandbags ahead of the rain at Halpatiokee Regional Park, 8303 SW Lost River Road, from noon to 6 p.m. Each household can receive up to 25 sandbags. Residents will be asked for their name and address. The county asks residents to check its map for the pickup location inside the park.

hero.headline: 18-year-old arrested in Port St. Lucie hit-and-run that critically injured scooter rider
hero.body:
An 18-year-old driver was arrested after police said he hit a woman riding an electric scooter to work in Port St. Lucie and drove away without stopping. Police identified him as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer and said he faces a felony charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. The 24-year-old woman was still unconscious and in critical condition Tuesday, Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said. “We're deeply concerned for her recovery, and our thoughts are with her loved ones,” he said. Published reports citing law enforcement records said Sanchez-Chasmer was being held on a $5,000 bond.

The collision occurred Monday morning near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Investigators said the woman was heading west along the sidewalk toward Southwest Rosser Boulevard. She had entered a crosswalk when a gray Chevrolet Tahoe turning left onto Southwest Feather Terrace hit her, according to police. She was wearing a helmet. A witness stopped to assist her, called 911 and recorded the SUV's license plate information. Police said investigators used that information to identify the vehicle and Sanchez-Chasmer as the driver. Two friends were riding with him at the time of the crash, investigators said.

Investigators said Sanchez-Chasmer and his friends had been playing “ding-dong-ditch” shortly before the collision. Niemczyk said they went to a friend's home and fled when the friend's mother answered the door. The chief said investigators believe those inside the Tahoe knew a collision had happened. Neither Sanchez-Chasmer nor either passenger called 911, according to Niemczyk. He said leaving rather than stopping to help was central to the criminal investigation. “Had they remained on scene, provided aid, it would have been a very different criminal outcome,” Niemczyk said. “There probably wouldn't have been criminal charges at that point.” Police have not announced charges against the passengers.

The crash also raised safety concerns for another young scooter rider who travels in the area. John Rogalewski, 15, said he rides an electric scooter to school and is sometimes out early in the morning. “I'm looking at my surroundings almost the whole time,” he said. “I'm making sure every time I have to cross the street that there's not a car coming up, and that it is my sign to go, no matter how long I have to wait to cross.” Police said the investigation into the collision remains open, and toxicology results are pending.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County schools close Wednesday as superintendent pledges flood review
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Schools canceled Wednesday classes with heavy rain in the forecast, and Superintendent Dr. Jon Prince promised to review the district’s decisions during the Nov. 2 flooding. The review follows criticism over a video showing a boy wading through chest-high water after getting off a school bus in Port St. Lucie.

Prince said the district will monitor the weather Wednesday and decide late Wednesday afternoon whether to cancel Thursday classes. He said the district will continue that approach until officials are sure students can safely return. Prince said he hopes Wednesday’s closure is an overreaction but does not want to take chances. “The ground is so saturated, but if the conditions worsen tomorrow, we don't want a repeat of what happened November 2,” Prince said.

The video from Nov. 2 shows the boy stepping off a school bus on SW Coleman Avenue and walking through floodwaters that reach as high as his chest. Critics have pointed to the video in questioning the district’s actions. Prince apologized Tuesday night for the stress families experienced. “It was very stressful for our families, and I certainly apologize for the stress that they went through on that day,” he said.

Prince said the flooding was unexpected and that decisions were based on information available at the time. He said every decision made that day is being analyzed. “We are going to review all our procedures, our policies to make sure that if there's anything that we could have done differently, that moving forward we will,” he said.

cards.headline: Free sandbag stations open in St. Lucie County ahead of heavy rain
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce’s two park locations are open daily from dawn to dusk. Residents must bring their own bags and shovels as crews check drainage systems and clear them.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County residents preparing for heavy rain this week can fill sandbags at free self-serve stations while public works crews check swales and drainage systems, clearing them to address potential flooding. The City of Fort Pierce is offering sand at Martin Luther King Jr. Dreamland Park and Jaycee Park. Both parks are open daily from dawn to dusk, and residents should bring their own bags and shovels.

The county also has self-service sandbag distribution points at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds West Parking Lot and Lawnwood Stadium Parking Lot. Residents must bring their own supplies and fill their own bags. Dickerson Infrastructure and Stewart Materials donated sand for the county locations.

Residents have been filling sandbags at Dreamland Park in Fort Pierce to protect their homes. Resident Lisa Powell said her ditches remained full after the last storm, with standing water reaching her yard. “My ditches are full from the last storm, they haven't gone down, so this could be very bad. The water is just still standing there, up to the yard.” Recent flooding left parts of the county submerged. Residents in the Creekside development were trapped inside, with some using kayaks to navigate flooded streets and others wading through the water.

Fredrick Reeves, whose home previously flooded, is using sandbags and mulch to block water from entering his house before the upcoming rain. During the earlier flooding, he tried to soak up the water with clothing as it entered his home. Reeves described the situation as “overwhelming.” Residents can find updates about precautions at St. Lucie County’s emergency management portal, www.readystlucie.org, or contact the Public Works Department for more information.

“We're deeply concerned for her recovery and our thoughts are with her loved ones,” Niemczyk said.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County estimates $60 million shortfall as crews prepare for flooding threat
cards.teaser: The preliminary estimate reflects Amendment 3’s additional homestead exemption. County crews are deploying again after storm work two weeks ago generated unbudgeted overtime.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County is estimating a $60 million revenue shortfall next fiscal year under Amendment 3, which increases the homestead exemption, as crews deploy for another threat of rain and flooding. County spokesman Erick Gill said the preliminary estimate comes as county leaders consider their budgets and the costs of storm preparation and response.

Gill said the estimated shortfall would grow to about $120 million once the exemption increases further. “We're looking at the early estimates in this next upcoming fiscal year to be about a $60 million shortfall and then about $120 million once the exemption goes up.”

Crews are being deployed across the county as they were two weeks ago, Gill said. He estimated that 50 to 100 staff members, including public works crews, worked in the field during that storm, generating unbudgeted overtime. “I think everybody is well aware now that this storm drain system was not designed for the flooding we're getting nowadays,” Gill said.

This week, the county offered residents free sand to bag as another round of November rain and flooding threatened Florida's east coast. Dickerson Infrastructure and Stewart Materials donated the sand. Gill said other services cost money, with the coming Amendment 3 tax cuts already on county leaders’ minds.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County crews clear drains as more rain threatens flood-hit areas
hero.body:
Public Works crews are clearing drainage blockages and lowering water levels where possible in St. Lucie County as another round of rain threatens areas still recovering from flooding earlier this month. Crews are also inspecting drainage systems and checking waterways. The National Weather Service has issued a flood watch from Tuesday afternoon through Friday evening, with 3 to 6 inches of rain forecast and higher amounts possible in some locations. The ground remains saturated, increasing the risk of flooding even if rainfall is lighter than during the early November storms.

St. Lucie County public schools and district offices will close Wednesday, Nov. 18, after the district dismissed students two hours early Tuesday over flooding concerns. All after-school activities, aftercare programs and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are canceled. District officials will monitor rainfall, flooding, road closures and access to schools, bus stops and transportation routes throughout Wednesday. A decision on school operations for Thursday, November 19, will be announced Wednesday evening. The district said the forecast supported Tuesday’s early dismissal to get students home before the heaviest rain. School scheduling decisions draw on forecasts and information from the National Weather Service and Emergency Operations Center.

Two weeks ago, floodwaters stranded cars, trapped families and forced some residents to wade through deep water. Near Oak Hammock K-8, 7-year-old Ella Ghodooshim walked through chest-deep water with her mother, Thassia Rodrigues. Rodrigues described how quickly the flooding overwhelmed the neighborhood as parents struggled to reach their children. “It was pretty scary and in a matter of minutes we had everything just flood,” she said. Rhett Linton, a parent who recalled kayaking through the flooded intersection during the previous storm, welcomed Tuesday’s early dismissal. “I'm super happy that they are stepping up and taking precautions,” Linton said.

Officials are urging residents to plan ahead, monitor forecasts and local alerts, and limit unnecessary travel. Drivers should never enter standing or moving water, which can stall a vehicle and cause costly engine damage. If drivers cannot tell how deep the water is, they should turn around and find another route. Residents can report flooding concerns to St. Lucie County at flooding@stlucieco.org.

cards.headline: Free self-service sandbag stations open in Fort Pierce and St. Lucie County
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce’s two park locations are open daily from dawn to dusk. Residents must bring their own bags and shovels. County stations also require residents to bring supplies and fill their own bags.
cards.body:
The City of Fort Pierce and St. Lucie County are offering free self-service sandbag stations as residents prepare for heavy rainfall this week. Residents must bring their own supplies and fill their own bags to help protect their homes from potential flooding.

Fort Pierce’s stations are at Martin Luther King Jr. Dreamland Park and Jaycee Park. Residents are advised to bring their own bags and shovels. Both parks are open daily from dawn to dusk. Residents have been filling sandbags at Dreamland Park in preparation for the rain.

The county’s self-service distribution points are at the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds West Parking Lot and Lawnwood Stadium Parking Lot. Residents must bring their own supplies and fill their own bags at those locations. Dickerson Infrastructure and Stewart Materials donated sand for the county stations.

Public works crews in St. Lucie County are checking swales and drainage systems ahead of more severe weather. They are also clearing them. Recent flooding left parts of the county submerged and residents in the Creekside development trapped inside. Some residents used kayaks to navigate flooded streets, while others waded through the water.

Resident Lisa Powell said water from the last storm remained in her ditches. “My ditches are full from the last storm, they haven't gone down, so this could be very bad. The water is just still standing there, up to the yard.”

Residents can visit St. Lucie County’s emergency management portal at www.readystlucie.org for updates about precautions to take. They can also contact the Public Works Department for more information.

hero.body:
An 18-year-old driver has been arrested on a felony charge after Port St. Lucie Police Department investigators say he struck a woman riding an electric scooter to work Monday morning and left the scene. Police identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer, who faces a charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. The 24-year-old woman remained unconscious and in critical condition Tuesday, Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said.

The crash happened near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Investigators said the woman was traveling west on the sidewalk toward Southwest Rosser Boulevard and had entered a crosswalk when a gray Chevrolet Tahoe turning left onto Southwest Feather Terrace struck her. Police said she was wearing a helmet. “We're deeply concerned for her recovery, and our thoughts are with her loved ones,” Niemczyk said.

A witness stopped to help the woman, called 911 and obtained the SUV's license plate information, police said. Investigators used that information to identify the vehicle and Sanchez-Chasmer. Niemczyk said investigators believe the people inside the SUV realized a collision had occurred. “They're aware that they hit something. I'll say that,” he said.

Investigators said Sanchez-Chasmer had two friends with him and had been playing a “ding-dong-ditch” prank shortly before the crash. Niemczyk said they had gone to a friend's house and fled when the friend's mother came to the door. The chief said leaving the crash scene was key to the criminal investigation. “Had they remained on scene, provided aid, it would have been a very different criminal outcome,” Niemczyk said. The investigation remains active, and toxicology results are pending, according to police.

cards.teaser: Tristan Sanchez Chasmer, 18, is being held on a $5,000 bond. Police say he left the scene after a crash that critically injured a 24-year-old woman riding her e-scooter to work.
cards.body:
An 18-year-old was arrested in connection with a Port St. Lucie hit-and-run that left a 24-year-old woman critically injured while riding her e-scooter to work early Monday. Tristan Sanchez Chasmer faces one count of fleeing the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury and is being held on a $5,000 bond.

The crash happened near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Body camera footage shows officers responding to the scene, where the woman was unconscious in the road. A witness called 911 and helped her before she was airlifted to a hospital. She remains in critical condition.

Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said the driver left the scene without stopping to render aid or contact law enforcement. Detectives identified the vehicle and traced it to Chasmer. According to Niemczyk, Chasmer and two passengers had just ding-dong ditched a home about a mile from the crash site. “He was trying to get away from playing a prank,” Niemczyk said.

Niemczyk said the two passengers got out of the truck shortly after the crash, but neither they nor the driver called 911. “They're aware that they hit something. I'll say that,” he said. The two passengers are not facing charges.

hero.headline: 18-year-old arrested after Port St. Lucie hit-and-run critically injures e-scooter rider
hero.body:
An 18-year-old driver has been arrested after police say he left a crash that critically injured a 24-year-old woman riding an e-scooter to work in Port St. Lucie. The woman was in a crosswalk on SW Feather Terrace when she was struck Monday morning, police said.

Police identified the driver as Tristan Ray Sanchez-Chasmer, 18. He is charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. The crash happened Nov. 16 at about 5:10 a.m. near the intersection of SW Gatlin Blvd. and SW Feather Terrace. The woman was on her way to the Wendy's where she works. She was rushed to a hospital and remained in critical condition and in a coma, police said.

A good Samaritan recorded the vehicle's license plate number and stopped to help the woman, according to police. Investigators used that information to determine that a Chevy Tahoe struck her and to identify Sanchez-Chasmer as the driver. Police said he had been playing a game of ding, dong, ditch with friends before the crash.

Katie Santana, a Port St. Lucie resident who lives near the intersection, expressed concern about the driver's decision to leave. “I think for somebody to just leave another human being on the side of the road who was possibly injured, to not stop and check on them, it's truly heartbreaking that somebody would make that decision,” Santana said. Police said the State Attorney's Office would decide whether Sanchez-Chasmer could face a more serious charge if the woman dies.

hero.headline: Heavy rain may disrupt Indian River County waste pickups, close disposal sites
hero.body:
Heavy rain and gusty winds may delay Waste Management curbside collections in Indian River County, where ongoing flooding and the threat of more heavy rain have kept the Emergency Operations Center at Level 2, or partial activation. The landfill and all five Customer Convenience Centers may close early or remain closed if conditions become unsafe. The county urges residents to keep collection carts out of flooded streets.

Waste Management collects recycling in blue carts countywide. Its garbage, yard waste and bulk waste collection services cover unincorporated Indian River County, Fellsmere, Sebastian and Indian River Shores. Residents in other cities and towns should check with their local governments for service updates. The potential collection delays come as the east-central Florida coast faces a Slight Risk, or Level 2 out of 4, for excessive rainfall. Localized flooding is possible, especially along the coast, and some areas could receive 4 inches or more of rain.

For collection day, the county recommends putting carts out by 6 a.m., keeping lids closed, bagging garbage and avoiding overfilled carts. Cardboard should be flattened and placed inside recycling carts, while yard waste should remain inside yard waste carts. Residents should bring carts back in as soon as possible after collection. Those instructions accompany the county’s warning against placing carts in the street when it is flooded, as heavy rain and gusty winds threaten to disrupt solid waste services.

Emergency services, human services and infrastructure partners are coordinating response and recovery efforts while the Emergency Operations Center remains partially activated. The county urges residents to avoid flooded roads and floodwaters, watch for rising water in low-lying areas, and monitor weather conditions and official updates. Officials across the region also urge residents to keep roadways clear for emergency responders and find a safe alternate route when they encounter flooding. Residents with flood-related questions or information can call the Emergency Information Center at 772-226-4000 during operating hours.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County, Fort Pierce offer self-service sand ahead of potential flooding
cards.teaser: Residents must bring their own bags and shovels to fill sandbags. County sand is available at two Fort Pierce locations while supplies last, and city stations are open daily from dawn to dusk.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County and the city of Fort Pierce are offering self-service sand for residents concerned about potential flooding. Residents must bring their own bags and shovels and be prepared to fill their own sandbags. County supplies are available while they last.

The county’s two distribution locations are the St. Lucie County Fairgrounds west parking lot, 5601 W. Midway Road, Fort Pierce, and the Lawnwood Stadium parking lot, 2000 Virginia Ave., Fort Pierce. County officials said Dickerson Infrastructure and Stewart Materials donated four truckloads of sand, with two truckloads delivered to each location. Residents should also bring any other supplies they need to fill their bags.

The City of Fort Pierce is offering free self-serve sandbag stations at Martin Luther King, Jr. 25th Street and at Jaycee Park, at S. Ocean Drive and Melaleuca Drive. Both parks are open daily from dawn to dusk. Residents using the city stations should bring their own bags and a shovel.

For additional information about city sand distribution, residents can contact the Fort Pierce Public Works Department at 772-467-3794. The county’s emergency management website also offers information about preparing for severe weather and flooding.

hero.headline: Martin County plans high-water rescue vehicle deployment as heavy rain threatens
hero.body:
Martin County is preparing for heavy rain and potential flooding starting Tuesday afternoon, and the sheriff’s office plans to station high-water rescue vehicles in areas most likely to flood. County officials anticipate rainfall totals of 3 to 6 inches, with some locations potentially receiving 8 to 12 inches. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office is coordinating with the county’s emergency operations center to track rainfall and determine which roads could become hard to navigate. Placing rescue vehicles near vulnerable areas would help deputies get to people who need help at home or become stranded in their vehicles, the agency said.

Deputies are warning drivers not to continue onto roads covered by water because the depth can be misleading and damage beneath the surface may not be visible. Anyone whose usual route floods should find a safe alternative or stay in a safe place until conditions allow travel. Residents should not bypass road barriers or venture into flooded areas to check water levels. Officials are also asking people to leave roads clear for emergency crews. Martin County Fire Rescue says households should be ready to leave if flooding endangers their homes or neighborhoods and should prepare emergency supplies for everyone in the household, including pets. The county’s Community Information Center will provide information about flooding.

Preparations are also underway elsewhere on the Treasure Coast. Indian River County’s emergency operations center remains partially activated at Level 2 as officials address existing flooding and the threat of additional rain. Emergency services, human services and infrastructure agencies are coordinating response and recovery work. Residents can call the county’s Emergency Information Center at 772-226-4000 during its operating hours with flood-related questions or information. Rain and strong winds could delay Waste Management collections, and residents should keep collection carts out of flooded streets. The county’s landfill and five Customer Convenience Centers could close early or stay closed if conditions become dangerous.

In St. Lucie County, the fire district has high-water vehicles and a rescue boat available for flooding emergencies. Free sand is available while supplies remain at the County Fairgrounds, 5601 W. Midway Road in Fort Pierce, in the west parking lot, and at Lawnwood Stadium, 2000 Virginia Ave. Residents must bring bags, a shovel and any other needed supplies. County public safety officials also advise securing tarps, outdoor furniture and other loose belongings. Northeast winds of 25 to 30 mph are forecast for Tuesday and Wednesday, with coastal gusts reaching 35 to 40 mph. Strong winds blowing onshore can also produce hazardous surf and rip currents.

cards.headline: Joe Namath's Lucky Shuck planned for Jensen Beach's Rio Marine Village
cards.teaser: The waterfront restaurant will join Rio Marine Village, which broke ground Thursday in Jensen Beach. The development’s first phase is scheduled for completion in late 2028.
cards.body:
Joe Namath is bringing a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse to Rio Marine Village in Jensen Beach. The 30-acre waterfront development in Martin County broke ground Thursday after more than five years of planning, with its first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028.

The restaurant, owned by Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica, will be among several waterfront dining and entertainment destinations at Rio Marine Village. Plans also call for a second outdoor dining concept.

"The Lucky Shuck has always been about good food, good people and being on the water," Namath said. "Rio Marine Village gives us a home right on the river, and I can't wait to see boats pulling up and families sitting down together."

The mixed-use development will feature 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina and more than a half-mile of public riverwalk. Other planned amenities include the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue, along with a public park, boardwalk and beach. Kayak and paddleboard rentals are also planned.

Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions. Construction is expected to begin this month.
