hero.headline: Teen arrested in Port St. Lucie hit-and-run that critically injured scooter rider
hero.body:
An 18-year-old driver has been arrested on a charge of leaving the scene of a Port St. Lucie crash that critically injured a 24-year-old woman riding an electric scooter, police said. Investigators identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer.

The crash happened Monday morning near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. According to investigators, the woman was riding west on the sidewalk toward Southwest Rosser Boulevard. As she entered the crosswalk, a gray Chevrolet Tahoe driven by Sanchez-Chasmer struck her while making a left turn onto Southwest Feather Terrace.

Police said Sanchez-Chasmer left the scene without stopping to render aid to the woman. He was arrested on a charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury.

The Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit identified Sanchez-Chasmer and located the Tahoe during its investigation. Investigators also learned that Sanchez-Chasmer had been playing “ding dong ditch” just before the crash, police said.

As the woman on the scooter entered the crosswalk, she was struck by the 18-year-old driver of a gray Chevrolet Tahoe making a left turn onto Southwest Feather Terrace. Police said the driver fled the scene and failed to stop to render aid to the woman. Lucie Police Department's Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer and located the vehicle through its investigation. hero.headline: St. Lucie County schools releasing students two hours early ahead of flood watch
hero.body:
Schools in St. Lucie County are releasing students two hours early Tuesday ahead of a flood watch that runs from Tuesday afternoon through Friday evening. Forecasters expect 3 to 6 inches of rain, with higher amounts possible in some locations, as crews clear drainage systems in areas still recovering from early November flooding. The school district is asking families to monitor its official channels for updates as weather conditions change.

The National Weather Service issued the flood watch for St. Lucie County. The ground remains saturated, increasing the risk of flooding even if rainfall is lighter than during the early November storms. Public Works crews are inspecting drainage systems, clearing blockages and lowering water levels where possible. Crews are also checking waterways as the next round of rain approaches.

Two weeks ago, floodwaters stranded cars, trapped families and forced some residents to wade through deep water. One video showed 7-year-old Ella Ghodooshim walking through chest-deep water with her mother near Oak Hammock K-8.

Officials are urging residents to plan ahead, monitor forecasts and local alerts, and limit unnecessary travel. Drivers should never enter standing or moving water because floodwater can stall a vehicle and cause costly engine damage. Drivers who cannot tell how deep the water is should turn around and find another route. Residents can report flooding concerns to St. Lucie County at flooding@stlucieco.org.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie faces renewed flood threat with 4 to 6 inches of rain forecast
hero.body:
Another 4 to 6 inches of rain could fall over the next few days in Port St. Lucie, threatening renewed flooding in neighborhoods still recovering from record rainfall two weeks ago. St. Lucie Public Schools announced a two-hour early release Tuesday.

County crews have been inspecting canals and drainage systems, clearing them ahead of the expected rain. Officials warn that the ground remains saturated from recent storms, meaning far less rain than usual could cause flooding in neighborhoods, streets and other low-lying areas. The school district announced the early dismissal to avoid a repeat of the flooding problems that affected students taking buses home earlier this month.

The earlier flooding stranded cars, trapped some families in their homes and forced others to wade through deep water. “It was horrible,” said Port St. Lucie resident Crisostomo Santiago Perez. “Water was on top of the cars almost, covering hoods.” With more heavy rain forecast, Perez said he planned to get supplies before flooding returned.

Freshman Noah Julian was among those caught in the earlier flooding. He stepped off his school bus to find his neighborhood along Coleman Avenue flooded. A video recorded by neighbor Martina Elieson spread quickly on social media, showing him swimming through floodwaters to reach his driveway. His father, Romeo Julian, expressed concern about alligators, snakes and sharp objects in the water.

Residents are encouraged to monitor local forecasts and prepare for changing conditions as the rain moves into the area.

hero.headline: Martin County sheriff weighs e-bike seizures, parent charges after Jensen Beach crash
hero.body:
The Martin County sheriff is considering seizing illegal e-bikes and pursuing criminal charges against parents who knowingly allow their children to ride them. The sheriff outlined the potential crackdown Monday after a Jensen Beach crash left a 14-year-old Port St. Lucie boy with catastrophic injuries.

The boy was struck Sunday near U.S. 1 and Northwest Goldenrod Road and was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center, where he was in stable condition, the sheriff said at a news conference. He and a friend had traveled roughly five miles from home on separate e-bikes before attempting to cross U.S. 1. The friend made it across, but a northbound vehicle with a green light struck the 14-year-old. The impact threw him approximately 50 feet, and his e-bike landed about 100 feet away.

Investigators determined the boy was riding a 3,300-watt electric bike, more than four times the 750-watt limit cited by the sheriff. The sheriff described the motorbike-style vehicle as illegal for street use. The boy was wearing a helmet, which the sheriff credited with helping him survive the crash.

The proposed seizures and potential charges against parents would represent tougher consequences following educational workshops, warnings and previous enforcement efforts. The sheriff said those efforts have failed to curb dangerous riding. Martin County has recorded 41 e-bike crashes this year, involving riders ranging in age from 7 to 80, according to the sheriff.

The Florida Highway Patrol is leading the crash investigation, with assistance from the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

hero.headline: Indian River County schools modify Tuesday schedule ahead of expected heavy rain
hero.body:
The School District of Indian River County will put all schools on a Modified Day schedule Tuesday because of anticipated heavy rainfall, the district announced Monday, Nov. 16. All extracurricular activities will conclude by 2:30 p.m. Extended Day will be available Tuesday morning but closed Tuesday afternoon.

Weather-related absences will be excused if conditions prevent students from attending school. “We understand that weather conditions may affect families differently across our community. Please make the decision that is safest for your family. If weather conditions prevent your child from attending school, the absence will be excused,” the district said in its Monday statement.

cards.headline: Martin County sheriff weighs illegal e-bike seizures, possible charges for parents
cards.teaser: The proposals follow a Jensen Beach crash that left a 14-year-old Port St. Lucie boy with catastrophic injuries. The sheriff said the boy was riding a 3,300-watt e-bike that was not street-legal.
cards.body:
The Martin County sheriff said Monday that deputies are considering seizing illegal e-bikes and pursuing criminal charges against parents who knowingly allow their children to ride them, following Sunday’s crash in Jensen Beach. A 14-year-old Port St. Lucie boy suffered catastrophic injuries when his e-bike collided with a vehicle near U.S. 1 and Northwest Goldenrod Road, the sheriff said.

At a Monday news conference, the sheriff described the tougher consequences as options under consideration. He said educational workshops, warnings and previous enforcement efforts have failed to curb dangerous riding. Martin County has recorded 41 e-bike crashes this year, involving riders ranging in age from 7 to 80, according to the sheriff.

The injured boy and a friend had traveled roughly five miles from home on separate e-bikes before attempting to cross U.S. 1, the sheriff said. The first teen made it across, but a northbound vehicle with a green light struck the 14-year-old. The impact threw the boy approximately 50 feet, and his e-bike landed about 100 feet away. He was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center and is now in stable condition.

Investigators determined that the boy was riding a 3,300-watt electric bike, more than four times the 750-watt limit cited by the sheriff. The sheriff described the motorbike-style vehicle as not street-legal. The boy was wearing a helmet, which the sheriff credited with helping him survive the crash.

The Florida Highway Patrol is leading the crash investigation, with assistance from the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

hero.headline: More heavy rain threatens Jensen Beach as Hyline Drive residents clean up after flooding
hero.body:
Another round of heavy rain is forecast this week as Jensen Beach residents begin cleaning up homes on Hyline Drive that were flooded for eight days. Residents worry renewed flooding could undo their progress as volunteers help remove damaged materials and treat homes for mold.

Susan Destafney’s home next to the Hyline Pond was filled with dirty floodwater for eight days. She said she lost almost everything, and volunteers are tearing the home down to the studs and treating it for mold. “Eight days of standing water. There was nothing that we could do but watch everything deteriorate and mold,” Destafney said.

County officials have pumped water from the neighborhood and the pond. They have also established a recovery assistance webpage for residents. Residents said crews are draining the Hyline Pond again as more rainfall approaches. Destafney said she is relying on volunteers and nonprofits for day-to-day needs during the cleanup.

Some belongings Destafney managed to save are on her back porch, leaving her worried about what the coming rain could do to them. She fears another flood could put her back at square one. “I've cried more than I've ever cried before. It's just a lot to take in, and it should never have happened,” she said.

Crystal van Duyme also expressed concern about the forecast as she and her friends work to recover. She said cleanup efforts have focused on getting the area dry after the floodwater receded, and the prospect of flash flooding has residents nervous about a repeat of the conditions they recently endured.

hero.headline: Rio Marine Village breaks ground in Jensen Beach with 342 apartments and marina
hero.body:
Rio Marine Village, a 30-acre mixed-use development in Jensen Beach, broke ground Thursday after more than five years of planning. The Martin County project will include 342 apartments, a 131-slip marina and more than a half-mile of public riverwalk.

Construction is expected to begin this month, with the first phase scheduled for completion in late 2028. Martin County commissioners unanimously approved the project's first two phases following years of community discussions.

Plans call for public waterfront access through a riverwalk, park, boardwalk and beach, along with kayak and paddleboard rentals. In addition to waterfront dining and entertainment destinations, the development will feature the Osprey Club, a waterfront wedding and event venue.

Among the restaurants will be a new location of The Lucky Shuck Oyster Bar & Taphouse, owned by football legend Joe Namath and his business partner Charlie Modica. A second outdoor dining concept is also planned.

“The Lucky Shuck has always been about good food, good people and being on the water,” Namath said. “Rio Marine Village gives us a home right on the river, and I can't wait to see boats pulling up and families sitting down together.”

hero.headline: St. Lucie Public Schools to dismiss two hours early Tuesday ahead of potential severe weather
hero.body:
St. Lucie Public Schools will dismiss students two hours early Tuesday, Nov. 17, ahead of potential severe weather and heavy rainfall. The district announced that schools will follow a two-hour early release schedule as forecasts call for more rain Tuesday, with heavier rainfall possible into the evening. Weather-related student absences will be excused, the district said.

School officials are asking parents and guardians to consider conditions in their neighborhoods and along their children’s routes to and from school. Weather conditions could vary significantly across St. Lucie County. The district said decisions about Tuesday’s after-school activities and athletics will be based on weather conditions, and it will release additional information as it becomes available.

Decisions about school closures for the remainder of the week remain pending. Current forecasts indicate heavier rainfall could continue Wednesday through Friday, potentially causing additional flooding and further impacts later in the week.

St. Lucie Public Schools said it is working with the Emergency Operations Center and National Weather Service to monitor forecasts, flooding, road conditions and other local impacts. Families are encouraged to monitor official St. Lucie Public Schools communications for updates.

hero.headline: Sebastian River Middle School town hall to weigh Wabasso School move, arts pathway
hero.body:
The School District of Indian River County will hold a public town hall Monday, Nov. 16, at Sebastian River Middle School to gather feedback on a proposed new home for Wabasso School and a shared-campus arts pathway in Sebastian. The meeting runs from 5:30 to 6:30 p.m.

Families, staff and community members are invited to hear details, ask questions and comment on the two facility proposals as part of InnovatED Phase 2. Both plans remain under review, with School Board consideration expected in December.

Wabasso School serves students with specialized needs. District leaders have described its current campus as at capacity and have discussed moving the program to the former Glendale Elementary site in Vero Beach. The proposed move would provide room for growth and specialized spaces for life skills and independent learning.

The arts pathway proposal involves Sebastian Elementary School of the Arts. Officials have said it could share the Sebastian River Middle School campus while remaining a separate school and maintaining its own identity.

Monday’s meeting is the latest in a series of InnovatED community sessions. Phase 1 included several school relocations, shared campuses and boundary adjustments. Those changes took effect for the 2026-27 school year after School Board approval in December 2025. Residents who cannot attend Monday’s town hall can submit questions or comments to the planning team.

hero.headline: 37th Stuart Air Show draws large weekend crowds, organizers say
hero.body:
The 37th Stuart Air Show drew large crowds throughout the weekend, organizers said, with an anticipated record turnout Sunday for Veterans Appreciation Day. The event brought together longtime attendees and young aviation fans for aircraft displays, family traditions and appreciation for veterans.

Organizers said the weekend started strongly with a drone and fireworks show Friday night. Chrissy Valvano described a great turnout for the opening night and said Sunday’s attendance was expected to set a record. “Sunday, we’re looking at a record turnout for Veterans Appreciation Day, and this weather could not be better.”

For Sarah Naylor, the event continued a family tradition. “The Stuart Air Show has been a part of our community for many years,” Naylor said. “We have many memories of coming in the past, as long as I can remember.”

Military aircraft were among the biggest attractions for young aviation fans Wyatt and Ivy Rotan. “I like coming to the Stuart Air Show because I like to see the C-17 and the F-16 fly,” Wyatt said. “I like seeing the C-17,” Ivy added.

John Gefell connected his visit with both aviation education and his family’s military service. Gefell said he was working on his aviation merit badge as a Boy Scout and that his grandfather was a veteran. “You get to have a lot of fun around here, just going around and seeing a bunch of planes,” he said.

hero.headline: Martin County postpones 25-firefighter hiring class despite 17 vacancies
hero.body:
Martin County has postponed a hiring class of 25 new firefighters while Fire Rescue is short 17 firefighters, citing projected property-tax revenue losses. The firefighters' union raised public-safety concerns about the staffing shortage and the decision to delay hiring.

County Administrator Don Donaldson confirmed that the class will not proceed as planned but said it was postponed, not canceled. He attributed the delay to budget uncertainty caused by Amendment 3, a measure recently approved by Florida voters that will lower property taxes statewide. Martin County estimates the amendment will result in a $75 million revenue loss over the next two years.

The union described the hiring class as canceled in a Thursday social media post that raised concerns about Fire Rescue staffing. “It is about public safety, firefighter working conditions, and ensuring Martin County residents receive the level of emergency services they pay for and deserve,” the post said.

Donaldson acknowledged those concerns. “I think the concern of the public is real and legitimate,” he said. He said the county needs to assess its budget before committing to new hires, citing the risk of hiring firefighters and then having to eliminate occupied positions.

“I don't want to have to lay somebody off six months right after I hire them,” Donaldson said. He said he hopes to have more clarity on firefighter hiring within the next few months.
hero.article_text: A day after the firefighters' union in Martin County expressed concerns about staffing, the County Administrator is responding by acknowledging the concerns while also saying there's not much that can be done right now. The union raised its concerns in a Thursday social media post, pointing out that the county had canceled an upcoming hiring class of 25 new firefighters even as Fire Rescue is understaffed. "It is about public safety, firefighter working conditions, and ensuring Martin County residents receive the level of emergency services they pay for and deserve," the post said. Don Donaldson, the county administrator for Martin County, acknowledged the union's concerns. "I think the concern of the public is real and legitimate," Donaldson said. Donaldson confirmed that fire rescue is already short-staffed by 17 firefighters and that the hiring class will not proceed as planned. However, he clarified that the class is postponed, not canceled. "I don't want to have to lay somebody off six months right after I hire them," Donaldson said. He explained that the delay is due to uncertainties in the county budget caused by Amendment 3, a measure recently approved by Florida voters that will lower property taxes statewide. Martin County estimates the amendment will result in a $75 million revenue loss over the next two years. Donaldson emphasized the need to assess the budget before committing to new hires. "What I didn't want to have happen is to fully fund all of our firefighters and then find we have to eliminate a position or two with somebody already in the position," Donaldson said. Donaldson said he hopes to have more clarification on the hiring of firefighters within the next few months. hero.headline: Town meeting planned on Jensen Beach flooding as families seek rebuilding help
hero.teaser: Residents will have a chance to question county, state and federal officials about flooding and assistance. Families are still removing mold-damaged materials and relying on volunteers and donations.
hero.body:
A town meeting is planned this week for Jensen Beach residents to ask county, state and federal officials about flooding and recovery assistance as families continue removing mold-damaged materials from their homes. Stephen Leighton, chief of staff for Brian Mast, R-Fla., said the question-and-answer meeting is planned as the community seeks clarity about the flooding and available help.

Weeks after floodwaters left several homes under feet of water, residents are removing damaged drywall, clearing debris and collecting donated supplies. Water marks remain visible on some homes. Volunteers, churches, firefighters, contractors and local leaders have joined the recovery effort as families work to make their homes livable again.

Homeowner Lisa Marie French, whose home was affected, has helped coordinate community cleanup efforts alongside Christ of Church, Family Church and other organizations. She said houses must be emptied and cleaned, with mold and damaged drywall removed. Neighbors and other volunteers have repeatedly arrived, asked what families need and started working. “People have been just coming and just hands-on,” French said.

Residents also want answers about what contributed to the flooding. Some are questioning whether pumping from Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce into the Savannas Preserve contributed to flooding in their neighborhood. Leighton said officials are working through those questions during the recovery process. “There's a lot of answers that these residents need, and hopefully we can do that,” he said. He also said the state had taken steps toward an emergency declaration and contacted the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA).

For French, rebuilding depends on assistance, donated materials and volunteer labor. She said her home is not in a flood zone and she does not have flood insurance. “We're trying to get any type of help. We don't have flood insurance here,” French said.

Residents say more volunteers are needed. Leighton said even helping families pack belongings can make a difference. “To help somebody take that picture off the wall and put it in a box, so they can move on, is a big deal,” he said.

cards.headline: Martin County postpones 25-firefighter hiring class despite 17 vacancies
cards.body:
Martin County has postponed a hiring class for 25 new firefighters while Fire Rescue is short-staffed by 17 firefighters. County Administrator Don Donaldson confirmed the delay, citing budget uncertainty and concerns about hiring employees the county might later have to lay off.

The firefighters' union raised staffing concerns in a Thursday social media post that described the class as canceled. Donaldson clarified that the class is postponed. The union said staffing affects emergency services for residents and working conditions for firefighters.

“It is about public safety, firefighter working conditions, and ensuring Martin County residents receive the level of emergency services they pay for and deserve,” the post said.

Donaldson attributed the delay to budget uncertainty caused by Amendment 3, a measure recently approved by Florida voters that will lower property taxes statewide. Martin County estimates the amendment will result in a $75 million revenue loss over the next two years. He said the county needs to assess its budget before committing to new hires.

“I don't want to have to lay somebody off six months right after I hire them,” Donaldson said. He said he wanted to avoid fully funding firefighter positions only to have to eliminate positions after employees had been hired.

Donaldson acknowledged the concerns about staffing, saying, “I think the concern of the public is real and legitimate.” He said he hopes to have more clarity on firefighter hiring within the next few months.

"It is about public safety, firefighter working conditions, and ensuring Martin County residents receive the level of emergency services they pay for and deserve," the post said. Don Donaldson, the county administrator for Martin County, acknowledged the union's concerns. "I think the concern of the public is real and legitimate," Donaldson said. Donaldson confirmed that fire rescue is already short-staffed by 17 firefighters and that the hiring class will not proceed as planned. However, he clarified that the class is postponed, not canceled. "I don't want to have to lay somebody off six months right after I hire them," Donaldson said. "What I didn't want to have happen is to fully fund all of our firefighters and then find we have to eliminate a position or two with somebody already in the position," Donaldson said. cards.headline: Stuart Air Show brings F-16 demonstrations, heavier traffic to Witham Field
cards.teaser: The 37th annual Stuart Air Show runs through Sunday at Witham Field, with military aircraft, aerobatic planes and skydivers on the program.
cards.body:
The 37th annual Stuart Air Show at Witham Field runs through Sunday, bringing aircraft, crowds and heavier traffic to the Stuart area. This year’s program features the F-16 demo team alongside large military planes, ghost riders, aerobatic planes and skydivers. Games and food are also part of the event’s offerings for families.

Among the participants is Maj. Taylor Hiester, the United States Air Force F-16 Viper Demonstration Team Commander and Pilot stationed at Shaw Air Force Base in Sumter, South Carolina. Hiester said he has served in the Air Force for 11 years and described the opportunity to connect with the public as a special part of his role. “To be the American fighter pilot that gets to connect the American people with the people that do their business around the world on their behalf, is very special,” he said.

Hiester described the Stuart appearance as his last performance of the year and said the event also closes out the year for many other performers. Beyond the flight demonstrations, the air show focused on education and STEM classes. Students involved included members of the aerospace club from Jupiter Christian, along with students from the Parker area, the Virginia Beach area, Fort Pierce and around the Treasure Coast.

The aviation lessons included how weather affects pilots. Students learned why pilots take off and land into the wind, how airflow over the wings helps provide lift, and how a strong tailwind can make a controlled landing more difficult. They also learned how icing can affect aircraft at high altitudes and near thunderstorms.
cards.article_text: The Stuart Air Show is preparing to take flight at Witham Field, bringing aircraft, crowds and heavier traffic to the Stuart area. The air show is celebrating its 37th year at Witham Field on Friday and this year’s event will feature the F-16 demo team along with a variety of other aircraft. The show runs through Sunday, Nov. Among those participating is Maj. Taylor Hiester, the United States Air Force F-16 Viper Demonstration Team Commander and Pilot stationed at Shaw Air Force Base in Sumter, South Carolina. “I’ve been in the Air Force for 11 years now, and it’s been a dream come true for the last three years to serve, not just as a military officer first, but fighter pilot second,” Hiester told WFLX Anchor Mike Trim. “To be the American fighter pilot that gets to connect the American people with the people that do their business around the world on their behalf, is very special.” The 37th annual air show features F-16s, large military planes, ghost riders, aerobatic planes and skydivers, along with games and food for families. “It’s for me, my last performance and for a lot of performers, it’s that it’s the close out of the year,” Hiester told WFLX. “So, it is a wonderful cocktail of emotions that come together that make a fantastic show for the people of Florida, and I think that the people are going to notice that there’s something special.” Beyond the flight demonstrations, the event also focused on education and STEM classes WFLX First Alert Weather Meteorologist Kate Wentzel spoke with students from the aerospace club from Jupiter Christian, along with students from the Parker area, the Virginia Beach area, Fort Pierce and around the Treasure Coast. “In the air show, they want to partner with all of these school groups and organizations, because really it empowers them and inspires them to go into aviation-related careers,” Wentzel said. Weather plays a critical role in aviation, and the students learned how it affects pilots. “We talked about winds, how that impacts pilots. Pilots want to take off into the wind, because the wind blowing over the wings, gives them better lift and a faster lift speed,” Wentzel said. “They also want to land into the wind, because if they have a tailwind pushing them too strong, it can make it difficult for the pilot to have a controlled landing.” Students also learned how icing can impact aircraft at high altitudes and near thunderstorms. Aircraft are supposed to stay 20 miles away from severe thunderstorms at all times, because that is where big updrafts and gusty winds develop, Wentzel said. Conditions are expected to be clear and breezy this evening, making for good viewing of the Stuart Air Show.

cards.headline: Martin County postpones 25-firefighter hiring class despite 17 vacancies
cards.body:
Martin County has postponed a hiring class of 25 new firefighters even as Fire Rescue is short-staffed by 17 firefighters, County Administrator Don Donaldson confirmed. The decision drew concerns from the firefighters' union about emergency services and working conditions. Donaldson said budget uncertainty prompted the delay and clarified that the class is postponed, not canceled.

Donaldson attributed the uncertainty to Amendment 3, a measure recently approved by Florida voters that will lower property taxes statewide. Martin County estimates the amendment will cost the county $75 million in revenue over the next two years. Donaldson said the county needs to assess its budget before committing to new hires. “I don't want to have to lay somebody off six months right after I hire them,” Donaldson said.

The union raised its staffing concerns in a Thursday social media post, describing the hiring class as canceled while pointing to Fire Rescue's staffing shortage. “It is about public safety, firefighter working conditions, and ensuring Martin County residents receive the level of emergency services they pay for and deserve,” the post said. Donaldson responded a day later, acknowledging the concerns. “I think the concern of the public is real and legitimate,” he said.

Donaldson said he wants to avoid filling positions that the county might later have to eliminate. “What I didn't want to have happen is to fully fund all of our firefighters and then find we have to eliminate a position or two with somebody already in the position,” he said. He hopes to have more clarity on firefighter hiring within the next few months.

The sheriff's office is asking those responding to the search to provide identifying information about the animal, rather than simply make a claim that the hog belongs to them.

A photo or description is the requested way to establish ownership. hero.headline: Driver killed in Fort Pierce I-95 crash after fleeing trooper; southbound lanes reopen
hero.body:
A 59-year-old DeLand man died Saturday morning when his car struck palm trees along I-95 in Fort Pierce after he fled a Florida Highway Patrol trooper and an attempted PIT maneuver failed, according to FHP. The southbound lanes have reopened, and a traffic homicide investigation remains ongoing.

A trooper spotted the man's 2020 Volvo S60 traveling south near Mile Marker 141 around 7:05 a.m. and clocked it at 101 mph, FHP said. The trooper attempted to pull the car over, but the driver refused to stop. He continued south at high speed, weaving through traffic and using the paved shoulders, according to FHP.

Troopers said an attempted PIT maneuver north of Okeechobee Road was unsuccessful. The driver continued speeding before veering onto the inside shoulder and into the grassy median, where the Volvo struck several large palm trees. The impact was on the driver's side and ejected the man. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

The crash shut down southbound I-95 for approximately five miles, forcing drivers off the interstate at Exit 129 for Okeechobee Road. The closure extended south to Mile Marker 124. Both entrance ramps from Okeechobee Road to I-95 South also closed before the interstate reopened.

FHP said the driver's next of kin has been notified.

cards.headline: Nearly 650 sign up for free youth heart screenings in Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: Ray and Cheryl Lalloo organized Saturday’s event in memory of their daughter, Jessica Clinton. Screenings are free for ages 5 to 20, and families can call about a waiting list.
cards.body:
Nearly 650 children have signed up for a free heart-screening event scheduled for Saturday at the St. Lucie County Health Department in Port St. Lucie. Organizers Ray and Cheryl Lalloo are honoring their daughter, Jessica Clinton, who died of cardiac arrest in 2003, and working to identify heart conditions that routine sports physicals may miss.

The screenings are available to children and young adults ages 5 to 20. They include an electrocardiogram (EKG) and a check of vital signs. A cardiologist reviews the results, and an echocardiogram is available if needed. The event is scheduled to begin at 8 a.m. at the St. Lucie County Health Department, 5150 NW Milner Dr. Appointments are booked, but families can call 772-462-3800 to ask about the waiting list. Organizers said they will try to fill openings when someone cancels or misses an appointment.

Jessica was 17 and at cheerleading practice at St. Lucie West Centennial High School when she went into cardiac arrest. She died that day. Her parents said she had undergone two sports physicals in the months before her death, but neither detected a heart problem. After losing their daughter, the Lalloos founded the Jessica Clinton MVP Foundation. They began offering heart screenings 17 years ago and said those screenings have helped identify previously undiagnosed conditions. Last year, about 19 children learned they had a previously undetected condition, the parents said.

Ray Lalloo stressed the importance of identifying heart problems early. The parents hope their work will prevent other families from experiencing a loss like theirs. “The one child could be the next president of our country. It could be the person who invents the cure for cancer. So, every life is important. Children should not die like this,” he said.

Martin County Fire Rescue, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office and the Florida Highway Patrol worked together to clear debris from the crash.

hero.headline: I-95 closed in both directions in Indian River County after fatal trooper-involved shooting
hero.body:
I-95 was shut down in both directions in Indian River County early Friday after a trooper-involved shooting left a suspect dead. Drivers were being diverted off the interstate at Indrio Road and Oslo Road as authorities investigated the shooting. FDLE will take over as the lead investigative agency.

Northbound drivers were being directed to exit at Indrio Road, while southbound drivers were being directed off at Oslo Road. The northbound entrance ramp from Indrio Road and the southbound entrance ramp at Oslo Road were also closed. The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office said the highway closure was due to the ongoing investigation.

FHP said the shooting occurred around 11:20 p.m. near mile marker 141. The incident began when a trooper initiated a traffic stop and the suspect fled, leading to a pursuit. The pursuit escalated into an exchange of gunfire between the trooper and the suspect, according to FHP.

The suspect sustained what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound and was pronounced dead at the scene, FHP said. Authorities said no troopers were injured. Officials said all body camera and dash camera video will be reviewed during the investigation.

hero.headline: Fatal crash closes southbound I-95 near Okeechobee Road in Fort Pierce
hero.body:
A fatal crash closed all southbound lanes of Interstate 95 near Okeechobee Road in Fort Pierce on Saturday morning. The Florida Highway Patrol confirmed that troopers were investigating the crash at the scene. Florida 511 listed the shutdown at Mile Marker 128, with the closure first reported shortly before 7:45 a.m. The shutdown was initially attributed to police activity before authorities confirmed that the incident involved a fatal crash. Drivers were urged to avoid the area and expect delays while the investigation continued along the southbound side of the interstate near Okeechobee Road.

The traffic closure covered every southbound lane at the reported location, according to Florida 511. For motorists traveling south on I-95, the shutdown affected the stretch near Okeechobee Road in Fort Pierce. The morning traffic report placed the closure at Mile Marker 128 and identified police activity as the initial reason for stopping traffic there. Authorities subsequently confirmed the fatal crash, and the Florida Highway Patrol said its troopers were investigating at the scene. The crash investigation was the reason for the southbound closure that prompted drivers to be advised to stay away from the area.

The first report of the lane shutdown came just before 7:45 a.m. Saturday. That report concerned the closure of the southbound lanes near Okeechobee Road, where the incident was first described as police activity. The later confirmation from authorities established that the incident was a fatal crash. Troopers were at the scene conducting their investigation as the southbound lanes were closed. The location identified by Florida 511, Mile Marker 128, put the traffic disruption on I-95 in Fort Pierce, near the same road referenced in the initial report of the morning shutdown.

Drivers were advised to avoid the affected area and allow for delays as the investigation continued. The warning accompanied a full closure of the interstate’s southbound lanes at Mile Marker 128, rather than a shutdown limited to a single southbound lane. The Florida Highway Patrol’s confirmation of a fatal crash followed the initial report that police activity had closed the roadway. For southbound motorists approaching the Okeechobee Road area, the reported closure and the advice to avoid it were the key traffic information Saturday morning, while troopers investigated the crash at the Fort Pierce scene.

hero.headline: Martin County postpones 25-firefighter hiring class despite 17 vacancies
hero.body:
Martin County has postponed a hiring class for 25 firefighters while its Fire Rescue department has 17 firefighter vacancies, County Administrator Don Donaldson confirmed. Donaldson said the county needs a clearer picture of its finances before moving ahead with the hires. The county projects a $75 million revenue loss over the next two years because of a recently approved state amendment affecting property taxes. The class will not go forward as planned, but Donaldson said it has been postponed rather than canceled. He hopes to have more clarity about firefighter hiring within the next few months.

The delay drew concern from the firefighters’ union, which described the class as canceled in a Thursday social media post. The union pointed to the department’s staffing shortage and said the issue involved public safety, firefighters’ working conditions and the emergency services residents pay for and should receive. Donaldson responded the following day, acknowledging the concerns while explaining the county’s financial uncertainty. “I think the concern of the public is real and legitimate,” he said. He confirmed both the 17 vacancies and the decision not to proceed with the upcoming class as originally planned.

Donaldson attributed the uncertainty to Amendment 3, which Florida voters recently approved and which will lower property taxes statewide. Martin County estimates the resulting reduction in its revenue will total $75 million over two years. Donaldson said he wants to assess the budget before committing to additional employees because he does not want to hire firefighters only to cut their jobs afterward. “I don't want to have to lay somebody off six months right after I hire them,” he said. His explanation centered on whether the county could maintain funding for the positions after bringing new firefighters into the department.

“What I didn't want to have happen is to fully fund all of our firefighters and then find we have to eliminate a position or two with somebody already in the position,” Donaldson said. He said the county needs to evaluate its funding before filling jobs it could later have to eliminate. For now, the hiring class remains postponed despite the existing staffing shortage. Donaldson’s hope is to get a clearer understanding of the hiring situation over the next few months as the county assesses its budget and the projected revenue reduction. The union’s concerns focus on staffing and services, while Donaldson said the hiring decision depends on that financial assessment.

cards.headline: Crash closed northbound Florida’s Turnpike in Palm City; truck slowed southbound traffic
cards.teaser: A crash near Mile Marker 137 closed northbound lanes Friday, while a jackknifed truck caused southbound congestion. Both drivers involved in the crash were safe.
cards.body:
A tractor-trailer and pickup truck crash closed all northbound lanes of Florida’s Turnpike near Mile Marker 137 in Palm City on Friday, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. A jackknifed truck caused southbound congestion from before Mile Marker 139 to before Mile Marker 137, according to Florida 511.

The crash happened just before 11 a.m. The crash-related northbound closure stretched from before Exit 133 for Stuart and Martin Downs Boulevard (State Road 714) to before Mile Marker 137. A separate closure for police activity extended from before Mile Marker 130 to Exit 133. The northbound on-ramp was also closed.

Both drivers involved in the crash were safe, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. Fire rescue, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office and Florida Highway Patrol were working to clear debris from the roadway.

Both drivers were safe, and no injuries were reported. Fire rescue, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office and Florida Highway Patrol were working to clear debris from the roadway. The crash happened just before 11 a.m. Northbound traffic was closed from before Exit 133 for Stuart and Martin Downs Boulevard (State Road 714) to before Mile Marker 137. A separate police activity closure extended from before Mile Marker 130 to Exit 133, and the northbound on-ramp was also closed. Southbound, a jackknifed truck was causing congestion from before Mile Marker 139 to before Mile Marker 137, according to Florida 511. Drivers were advised to take alternate routes and expect delays. hero.headline: FHP revises account of fatal I-95 shooting in Indian River County; lanes reopen
hero.body:
FHP said Friday that investigators have not determined who fired the shot that killed a man during a pursuit involving trooper gunfire on I-95 in Indian River County, revising its initial account that his wound appeared self-inflicted. All northbound and southbound lanes have reopened after the incident shut down the interstate for several hours near the Indian River-St. Lucie County line.

At a 2 p.m. news conference, FHP said the fatal shot remained under investigation. The Florida Department of Law Enforcement is investigating, and the two FHP troopers involved are on paid administrative leave pending the outcome. The man was pronounced dead at the scene.

The shooting occurred about 11:20 p.m. Thursday near mile marker 141, according to FHP. The incident began when a trooper stopped a man driving over 90 mph near mile marker 138. Lt. Indiana Miranda said the trooper explained the reason for the stop and asked for the driver's license and registration. Miranda described the driver as hostile and said he cursed at the trooper. A second trooper arrived as backup and also asked for the man's driver's license. FHP said the man then accelerated and fled, prompting a pursuit.

During the pursuit, the man fired a gun at troopers, and one trooper returned fire while driving, according to FHP. “He said over the radio that there were shots being fired at them. Our trooper returned fire, while driving his vehicle and he was able to engage in a PIT,” Miranda said. FHP said troopers used a PIT maneuver that caused the man's vehicle to crash and roll over. Authorities said neither trooper was injured in the shooting.

Indiana Miranda gives update after man dies in trooper-involved shooting incidentOn Thursday, at about 11:20 p.m., FHP said a trooper was involved in a shooting incident on I-95 near mile marker 141. According to FHP, the incident began when the trooper initiated a traffic stop for a man driving over 90 mph near mile marker 138. Another trooper joined as back up and that's when, FHP said, the man got aggressive and was uncooperative. "The primary trooper who completed the stop addressed the driver and advised him the reason for the stop was the speed, asked him for his driver's license and registration, he noticed that the driver was hostile," Lt. Indiana Miranda said during a press conference on Friday. "There was a little bit of back and forth between the two, at which point the driver says, 'I don't want to talk to you,' and there was cursing by the driver to our primary trooper."The second trooper stepped in, asking for the man's driver's license as well. That is when the man accelerated and fled the traffic stop, resulting in a pursuit. The pursuit escalated, when the suspect fired a gun at troopers, with one of the troopers returning fire."He said over the radio that there were shots being fired at them. Our trooper returned fire, while driving his vehicle and he was able to engage in a PIT," Miranda said.FHP said the officers used a PIT maneuver causing the suspect to crash and rollover. Authorities said no troopers were injured during the shooting. The suspect was pronounced dead at the scene. FHP initially said the suspect sustained injuries from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. However, during the 2 p.m. press conference, FHP said that it is not clear who fired the shot that killed the suspect and that is under investigation.FHP said the Florida Department of Law Enforcement is investigating and the two FHP troopers are currently on paid administrative leave pending the outcome of the investigation.All northbound and southbound lanes of I-95 were closed for several hours into the morning. All lanes have since reopened.

hero.headline: Florida’s Turnpike northbound lanes reopen after crash near Palm City
hero.body:
All northbound lanes of Florida’s Turnpike near Palm City in Martin County have reopened after a crash involving a tractor-trailer and a pickup truck closed them for an hour Friday. The closure caused a backup of nearly 10 miles.

The crash happened just before 11 a.m. near mile marker 137, according to Martin County Fire Rescue. The agency reported that both drivers were safe with no reported injuries, while the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reported minor injuries and significant damage to both vehicles.

Martin County Fire Rescue, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office and the Florida Highway Patrol worked together to clear debris from the crash.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County rejects land-use change that could allow nearly 500 homes
hero.body:
St. Lucie County commissioners voted 3-2 to reject a land-use change that could allow nearly 500 homes on roughly 34 acres near South 25th Street and West Midway Road. The decision came amid concerns about drainage at the low-lying property as Creekside and White City residents sought answers about recent flooding.

An engineer said the property receives drainage from about 134 acres and uses a 24-inch pipe to direct water to nearby canals. Another pipe might be needed. The site sits lower than surrounding roads and would need to be raised for development, prompting concerns that construction could push water onto nearby properties.

A residential designation could allow up to 15 homes per acre, according to the discussion. County staff recommended approving the land-use change with adjustments to avoid or reduce impacts to wetlands and required buffers. Commissioners denied the request.

At the same meeting, residents from Creekside and White City asked commissioners to investigate recent flooding, identify who is responsible for local drainage systems and explain how to prevent future flooding. Creekside residents called for an engineering review of the neighborhood and surrounding watershed, a reassessment of flood risk and a mitigation plan with deadlines. They also requested a public meeting with county engineers and stormwater officials.

White City residents described recurring flooding and called for drainage improvements and more stormwater storage. One resident said her home and yard had flooded four times since 2012. The county also made its emergency declaration official after days of heavy rain and flooding. The declaration covers hazards including flooded roads and strained drainage systems.

cards.headline: Stuart Air Show runs through Nov. 15 at Witham Field, with heavier traffic expected
cards.teaser: The 37th annual show features the F-16 demonstration team, military aircraft, aerobatic planes and skydivers. Crowds are expected to bring heavier traffic to the Stuart area.
cards.body:
The Stuart Air Show runs through Sunday, Nov. 15, at Witham Field, bringing aircraft, crowds and heavier traffic to the Stuart area. Celebrating its 37th year at the airport, the event features the United States Air Force F-16 Viper Demonstration Team alongside a lineup of large military planes, ghost riders, aerobatic planes and skydivers. Games and food are also part of the offerings for families. Conditions are expected to be clear and breezy in the evening, making for good viewing of the show.

Among the participants is Maj. Taylor Hiester, the F-16 Viper Demonstration Team commander and pilot, who is stationed at Shaw Air Force Base in Sumter, South Carolina. Hiester has served in the Air Force for 11 years and described the opportunity to connect Americans with military personnel serving on their behalf as a special part of his role. The Stuart appearance is his final performance of the year and marks the season’s close for many other performers. “It is a wonderful cocktail of emotions that come together that make a fantastic show for the people of Florida, and I think that the people are going to notice that there’s something special,” Hiester said.

Beyond the flight demonstrations, the event includes education and STEM classes. Students involved in aviation weather lessons included members of the aerospace club from Jupiter Christian, along with students from the Parker area, the Virginia Beach area, Fort Pierce and elsewhere around the Treasure Coast. Meteorologist Kate Wentzel said the air show’s partnerships with school groups and organizations are intended to empower students and inspire them to pursue aviation-related careers.

The weather lessons covered how wind affects takeoffs and landings. Wentzel explained that pilots want to take off into the wind because airflow over the wings provides better lift. They also want to land into the wind, since a strong tailwind can make a controlled landing difficult. Students learned how icing can affect aircraft at high altitudes and near thunderstorms. Wentzel said aircraft are supposed to remain 20 miles away from severe thunderstorms at all times because of the large updrafts and gusty winds that develop there.

The show runs through Sunday, Nov. 15.WATCH BELOW: What to know about traffic, parking and getting to Witham FieldAmong those participating is Maj. Taylor Hiester, the United States Air Force F-16 Viper Demonstration Team Commander and Pilot stationed at Shaw Air Force Base in Sumter, South Carolina."I've been in the Air Force for 11 years now, and it's been a dream come true for the last three years to serve, not just as a military officer first, but fighter pilot second," Hiester told WPTV Anchor Mike Trim. "To be the American fighter pilot that gets to connect the American people with the people that do their business around the world on their behalf, is very special."The 37th annual air show features F-16s, large military planes, ghost riders, aerobatic planes and skydivers, along with games and food for families."It's for me, my last performance and for a lot of performers, it's that it's the close out of the year," Hiester told WPTV. "So, it is a wonderful cocktail of emotions that come together that make a fantastic show for the people of Florida, and I think that the people are going to notice that there's something special."Beyond the flight demonstrations, the event also focused on education and STEM classesWPTV First Alert Weather Meteorologist Kate Wentzel spoke with students from the aerospace club from Jupiter Christian, along with students from the Parker area, the Virginia Beach area, Fort Pierce and around the Treasure Coast. "In the air show, they want to partner with all of these school groups and organizations, because really it empowers them and inspires them to go into aviation-related careers," Wentzel said.Weather plays a critical role in aviation, and the students learned how it affects pilots"We talked about winds, how that impacts pilots. Pilots want to take off into the wind, because the wind blowing over the wings, gives them better lift and a faster lift speed," Wentzel said. "They also want to land into the wind, because if they have a tailwind pushing them too strong, it can make it difficult for the pilot to have a controlled landing."Students also learned how icing can impact aircraft at high altitudes and near thunderstorms. Aircraft are supposed to stay 20 miles away from severe thunderstorms at all times, because that is where big updrafts and gusty winds develop, Wentzel said.Conditions are expected to be clear and breezy in the evening, making for good viewing of the Stuart Air Show.

hero.headline: Florida releases all 20 names in voter fraud sweep as cases raise legal questions
hero.body:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier’s office released the names of all 20 defendants charged in a statewide voter fraud sweep this week after repeated requests, nearly seven weeks after announcing the arrests. At least eight cases involving noncitizens cite a law enacted after the defendants allegedly voted.

Uthmeier announced the sweep in September, before the midterm elections, and his office initially named 12 defendants. The full list spans 13 counties and includes 16 noncitizens and four convicted felons. The attorney general’s office said all 20 were ineligible to vote when they allegedly cast ballots. In response to questions about the law cited in the noncitizen cases, a spokesperson for the office said those investigations remain pending.

Among the defendants is Astrid Quintana, a lawful permanent resident charged in Lee County who has lived in the country since she was a toddler. Her attorney, Connor Martin, said she received a voter ID card before voting in 2024 and believed she could vote. “She had no intention to deceive anybody or to do anything that she believed was illegal,” Martin said. Her case and at least seven others involving noncitizens cite a law that did not exist at the time of the alleged voting. Asked whether the state could charge her under that law, Martin said, “Well, they cannot.”

The list also includes Mei-Lin Johnston, identified among the noncitizen defendants, with charges filed in Okeechobee County, and Jivonn Ysbeck, identified among the convicted felons, with charges filed in Palm Beach County. Duval County has the most cases, with four, followed by Hillsborough County with three.

In Hillsborough County, defendant Donta White remains on probation for grand theft and is ineligible to vote. The state said White, a father of two, admitted registering to vote twice and voting early in 2024. His attorney, Lynley Flagler, said he also received a voter ID card. “I feel that there's an entrapment issue,” Flagler said. “They want to prosecute voting, but they have not put any checks and balances in place to let people know when they're able to vote and when they can't vote.”

hero.headline: I-95 closed in both directions in Indian River County after fatal trooper-involved shooting
hero.body:
I-95 is closed in both directions in Indian River County following a trooper-involved shooting that ended with a suspect dead, authorities said. Northbound drivers are being directed off the interstate at Indrio Road, while southbound drivers are being directed to exit at Oslo Road.

All northbound and southbound lanes are closed, along with the southbound entrance ramp at Oslo Road and the northbound entrance ramp from Indrio Road. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said the highway closure is due to the ongoing investigation.

FHP said the shooting occurred around 11:20 p.m. near mile marker 141. The incident began when a trooper initiated a traffic stop and the suspect fled, leading to a pursuit, according to FHP. The pursuit escalated into an exchange of gunfire between the trooper and the suspect.

The suspect suffered what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound and was pronounced dead at the scene, FHP said. Authorities said no troopers were injured. FDLE will take over as the lead agency in the investigation, and officials said all body camera and dash camera video will be reviewed.

hero.headline: Woman, 75, killed by pickup while crossing Seaway Drive in Fort Pierce
hero.body:
Fort Pierce police said Friday that a 75-year-old woman died after a pickup truck struck her while she was crossing Seaway Drive with her husband. The crash remains under investigation, and police are asking anyone with information to come forward.

Officers responded Wednesday to the 1100 block of Seaway Drive. Police determined the couple were crossing toward the Dockside Inn Resort when a westbound 2013 Ford F-150 pickup truck driven by a man struck the woman. Her husband was uninjured, police said. The woman was taken to a local hospital, where she was pronounced dead at approximately 7 p.m.

Anyone with information about the crash is asked to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at www.tcwatch.org.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie sets Dec. 12 groundbreaking for new 6,000-seat soccer stadium
cards.teaser: The stadium at Walton & One will be fully funded by the development group under a land-use agreement with the city. The club is preparing to compete in USL League One in 2027.
cards.body:
A groundbreaking ceremony for a new 6,000-seat soccer stadium in Port St. Lucie is scheduled for noon Saturday, Dec. 12, at Walton & One. The club announced the construction plans Thursday as it prepares to compete in USL League One in 2027.

The stadium will occupy approximately six acres. The development group will fully fund construction and has entered into an agreement with the City of Port St. Lucie to use the land. Plans call for the stadium to serve as a year-round destination for families and community members, with entertainment and other events in addition to soccer.

Gustavo Suárez, the club’s founder and CEO, said the project is intended to become part of the community. “We set out to create something that feels like a true part of this community, a place where families can gather, young players can dream, and new traditions can take shape.”

The groundbreaking ceremony will bring together club leaders, USL representatives, partners and founding members. A public celebration will follow at 1:30 p.m., featuring food trucks, entertainment and activities for all ages. The club says it will announce more event details in the coming weeks.

cards.headline: Collin O’Hara sentenced to life for Calvin Bates’ 2020 killing in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: A judge denied the defense’s request for a reduced sentence. A jury had found O’Hara guilty of second-degree murder in Bates’ stabbing death.
cards.body:
Collin O’Hara was sentenced to life in prison Tuesday for the 2020 killing of Calvin Bates in Fort Pierce. The judge denied the defense’s request for a reduced sentence. A jury had found O’Hara guilty of second-degree murder, and he will receive credit for 3,341 days already served.

Fort Pierce police found Bates on a rear patio at an apartment complex at 601 Avenue B on June 12, 2020, with a knife in his neck. Bates later died during surgery at Lawnwood Hospital.

According to the arrest affidavit, a witness told investigators that O’Hara accused Bates of being a child rapist before stabbing him. Another witness said she saw O’Hara’s arm move toward Bates’ neck, then saw the knife in Bates’ neck as O’Hara left.

Police said O’Hara fled the scene and was arrested at an Anytime Fitness on Orange Avenue. During an interview with investigators, O’Hara denied stabbing Bates, according to the affidavit.

cards.headline: Cleanup begins near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach as floodwater slowly recedes
cards.teaser: Martin County pumping has allowed some homeowners to begin cleanup after more than a week of flooding. Recovery assistance is available at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach.
cards.body:
Residents near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach have begun cleaning out flood-damaged homes after Martin County started pumping water from the neighborhood Monday. The pumping allowed some homeowners to assess damage after more than a week of standing water, while other residents were still waiting for floodwaters to recede.

Lisa French, her husband and several neighbors began removing damaged drywall, tearing out the kitchen and carrying ruined furniture and belongings into the front yard early Wednesday. Floodwater had reached more than a foot deep in some rooms of French’s home. The water has receded from the house, but much of what she owns has been destroyed. “You know, you’re sitting there with your house full of water, sitting in the fact that you lost your entire home. But now we can actually move and work instead of think,” French said.

Other residents continued to wait for relief. Susan Destafney, who has lived in the neighborhood for four decades, said the flooding was unlike anything she had experienced there. “We’ve lived in our home for 40 years. We’ve never seen the likes of this,” Destafney said.

Community volunteers have been collecting cleaning supplies and other necessities for affected families. Alaura Macpherson, who runs the local group Quit Messen With Jensen, is organizing a community fundraiser and meal on Nov. 25 to raise money for flood victims. Local restaurants are expected to donate food. The event is also planned as a resource center to connect residents with contractors, cleanup services and other recovery assistance. “The community is what helps each other. We are a family,” Macpherson said. Martin County officials have also opened a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach to connect flood victims with recovery assistance.

cards.headline: Stuart Air Show access: Monterey Road entrances, free parking at Witham Field
cards.teaser: Visitors can use two drive-in entrances off Monterey Road, with free designated parking and complimentary shuttles to the main gates.
cards.body:
Visitors heading to the Stuart Air Show at Witham Field will have two drive-in entrances off Monterey Road, free general parking in designated areas and complimentary shuttles to the main gates. The Martin County Sheriff's Office will direct traffic around the air show, which is preparing to bring aircraft, crowds and heavier traffic to the Stuart area.

Drivers coming from Interstate 95 can take the Stuart exit and follow Kanner Highway to Monterey Road. Those using Florida's Turnpike can take Southwest Martin Downs Boulevard. Dixie Highway is another option for reaching Monterey Road. As visitors approach Witham Field, they should follow posted signs and directions from law enforcement.

General parking is free in designated Stuart Air Show parking areas, and ADA parking is available. Complimentary shuttles will carry visitors from the parking areas to the main gates. Drivers should use the official parking lots rather than create their own spaces or park outside designated areas.

cards.headline: Newly released 911 account details gun allegations in September Palm City standoff
cards.teaser: A woman told dispatchers Darrel Abbey was chasing her with guns and had fired them. Newly released sheriff’s office video shows deputies and a tactical vehicle at the property.
cards.body:
A newly released 911 call transcript adds details to September’s hourslong standoff in Palm City, with a woman telling dispatchers that Darrel Abbey was chasing her with guns and had fired them. The transcript, released through a public records request, describes the caller’s allegations during an incident that brought Martin County Sheriff’s Office deputies, SWAT team members and hostage negotiators to the home.

The woman urged dispatchers to send help quickly and said she was running down the street. She described Abbey as intoxicated and said he had tried to get into a car. About an hour and a half earlier, she told the dispatcher, Abbey had put a gun to his head and pulled the trigger, but the gun did not fire. She said he was not in a good state of mind.

As she ran, the caller said Abbey turned around and headed back toward the home. She stopped along the road, where another woman had pulled over to help her. The caller also said there were multiple guns at the property, though she was unsure whether they were inside the house, in a vehicle or in an RV. Separately, newly released sheriff’s office video shows deputies and a tactical vehicle at the property during the response. The footage is partially obscured.

According to the arrest report, Abbey’s ex-girlfriend went to his home after their breakup. She told investigators he appeared intoxicated and had a rifle in his Tesla and a 10 mm handgun in his shorts. The report says he brought the guns inside, yelled at her and pointed a gun at her several times. It also says he later tried to get into his vehicle and reached for her phone when he realized she was recording. She ran down the road and called 911.

Deputies later tried to contact Abbey at the home, but he refused to open the door or speak with them, according to the arrest report. He was booked into the Martin County Jail without bond on charges including battery and aggravated assault with a deadly weapon without intent to kill. The report identifies him as a convicted felon with a prior vehicular assault conviction in Washington state.

hero.headline: Groundbreaking set for Dec. 12 at 6,000-seat soccer stadium in Port St. Lucie
hero.body:
A groundbreaking ceremony for a new 6,000-seat soccer stadium at Walton & One in Port St. Lucie is scheduled for noon Dec. 12. The development group will fully fund construction and has entered into an agreement with the City of Port St. Lucie to use the land.

The club announced Thursday that construction will begin at the site, where the stadium will occupy approximately six acres. The team is preparing to compete in USL League One in 2027. Plans call for the stadium to serve as a year-round destination for entertainment and other events, as well as soccer.

Gustavo Suárez, the club’s founder and CEO, said the project is intended to become part of the community. “We set out to create something that feels like a true part of this community, a place where families can gather, young players can dream, and new traditions can take shape.”

The Dec. 12 groundbreaking will bring together club leaders, USL representatives, partners and founding members. A public celebration will follow at 1:30 p.m., with food trucks, entertainment and activities for all ages.

hero.headline: FDLE to investigate fatal encounter after I-95 pursuit in Indian River County
hero.body:
A suspect died after a pursuit and exchange of gunfire with an FHP trooper on I-95 in Indian River County, according to FHP. Both directions of the highway were closed early Friday for the investigation, which FDLE will lead.

FHP said the encounter began when a trooper initiated a traffic stop and the suspect fled. The pursuit escalated into an exchange of gunfire near mile marker 141 around 11:20 p.m. The suspect sustained what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound and was pronounced dead at the scene, FHP said.

The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said the highway closure was due to the investigation. Northbound drivers were being directed off I-95 at Indrio Road, while southbound drivers were being directed to exit at Oslo Road. The northbound entrance ramp from Indrio Road and the southbound entrance ramp at Oslo Road were also closed early Friday.

Officials said all body camera and dash camera video will be reviewed during the investigation. FDLE will take over as the lead investigative agency.

cards.headline: Collin O’Hara sentenced to life for 2020 killing of Calvin Bates in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: A judge denied the defense’s request for a reduced sentence. O’Hara will receive credit for 3,341 days already served.
cards.body:
Collin O’Hara was sentenced to life in prison Tuesday for the 2020 killing of Calvin Bates in Fort Pierce, with the judge denying the defense’s request for a reduced sentence. A jury found O’Hara guilty of second-degree murder. He will receive credit for 3,341 days already served.

Fort Pierce police found Bates on a rear patio at an apartment complex at 601 Avenue B on June 12, 2020, with a knife in his neck. Bates later died during surgery at Lawnwood Hospital.

According to the arrest affidavit, a witness told investigators O’Hara accused Bates of being a child rapist before stabbing him. Another witness said she saw O’Hara’s arm move toward Bates’ neck, then saw the knife in Bates’ neck as O’Hara left.

Police said O’Hara fled the scene and was arrested at an Anytime Fitness on Orange Avenue. During an interview with investigators, O’Hara denied stabbing Bates, according to the affidavit.

cards.headline: Martin County plans to revive drainage project as flooding persists in Trailside
cards.teaser: Residents describe 3 to 4 feet of water covering parts of Hungryland Farms. The county plans to advance a drainage project designed years ago as residents renew concerns dating to 2018.
cards.body:
Floodwater continues to cover parts of Trailside in western Martin County, where county officials plan to revive a drainage project after a berm breach sent water toward the community. Residents describe 3 to 4 feet of water across parts of Hungryland Farms, forcing cattle to wade and swim through submerged pastures. Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said a berm breached Monday on the county-owned Elise J Property northeast of Trailside, sending water into a nearby canal, with some flowing back into the community. High water has kept crews from reaching the breach, he said.

The flooding follows years of warnings from residents. In a 2018 letter, Trailside Homeowners Association President Kyla Shay warned homeowners that property south of Trailside had effectively become a reservoir, with water rising as much as 3.5 feet above community roads and breaching a berm. That year, she also contacted the South Florida Water Management District, warning that blocked drainage had left some pastures under 8 feet of water. Shay said the underlying problems persisted. “It's a combination of years of 'We'll get to it,' and we never got to it,” she said.

Engineer Bob Higgins, who works with the Pal Mar Water Control District and the Hobe St. Lucie Conservancy District, said an outfall designed years ago would allow water to drain through the R G Mitigation Bank Preserve to the south and the neighboring Elise J property. Martin County acquired that property in 2026. Gorton said county officials discussed a formal water control structure with the former owner and that the owners submitted two permit applications to the South Florida Water Management District. The project was never built. The district said Trailside was outside its jurisdiction, while Gorton said it had permitted every property within Trailside and oversaw the proposed drainage project.

Gorton said Trailside is surrounded by berms, hundreds of acres of wetlands and two independent water control districts, with only one drainage ditch allowing water to escape slowly. He has requested the original permit applications to help expedite approval and construction. Gorton plans to return Friday to assess flooding and possible immediate relief. “The good news is the county purchased that property, and it's our intent to bring that project forward,” he said. At Hungryland Farms, submerged pastures have left cattle without their primary food source, and a farmer said the water continued rising after the rain stopped.

They say it's a crisis years in the making — one they warned officials about as far back as 2018.Documents obtained by WPTV show residents raised concerns about drainage problems long before last week's historic rainfall inundated the Treasure Coast.Now, with the rain gone but the water lingering, residents are questioning whether the devastation could have been prevented.Melissa, who raises grass-fed cattle at Hungryland Farms in the rural Trailside community, says the flooding has transformed her property almost overnight."It feels like Lake Okeechobee," she said.Her cattle, accustomed to grazing freely across the farm, are now navigating deep floodwater. "It's completely covered," Melissa said. they're all underwater."The flooding has left her animals without their primary food source and exposed them to potentially deadly hazards, including drowning, waterborne parasites and electrical dangers.Melissa pointed to an electrical transformer nearly submerged by floodwater, questioning whether her cattle could be electrocuted if they wandered too close.And despite the rain stopping, she said the water isn't draining — it's rising. said.Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton acknowledges the community faces significant drainage challenges.Gorton said a berm breached Monday on the county-owned Elise J Property northeast of Trailside, sending water into a nearby canal, with some water backflowing into the community."We still can't get back to that breach," Gorton told investigative reporter Kate Hussey, explaining that high water levels have prevented crews from accessing the area.But the larger problem, he said, is Trailside's geography.The community is essentially a bathtub, surrounded by berms, hundreds of acres of wetlands and two independent water control districts.Water flows into the area, but there is only one drainage ditch for it to slowly escape."There's no easy way to get that water out except by pump or gravity," Gorton said.WPTV contacted engineer Bob Higgins, who works with both the Pal Mar Water Control District and the Hobe St. Lucie Conservancy District.Higgins said a potential solution had already been designed years ago: an outfall that would allow water to drain through the R G Mitigation Bank Preserve to the south and the neighboring Elise J property, which Martin County acquired in 2026. But that project was never built.When Hussey asked Gorton whether the county had been aware of the proposal, he confirmed officials had discussed it with the property's former owner."We did have some dialogue with the previous owner of Elise J about creating a formal water control structure that could discharge before the berms would breach," Gorton said.According to Gorton, the former owners submitted two permit applications to the South Florida Water Management District, but construction never began.WPTV contacted the former property owners, who said they did not know why the project was never completed.When Hussey reached out to the South Florida Water Management District, the agency said Trailside was outside its jurisdiction.However, Gorton said the district had permitted every property within Trailside and oversaw the proposed drainage project.Hussey followed up with the district, seeking clarification about its jurisdiction and asking why the drainage project was never constructed.The district has not responded to those follow-up questions.Despite the years of delays, Gorton said there may finally be a path forward."The good news is the county purchased that property, and it's our intent to bring that project forward," he said.Gorton said he has already requested the original permit applications in hopes of expediting approval — and construction— of the project.He also plans to return Friday to assess the flooding and determine what immediate relief may be possible."We're looking at ways to get the water out faster," he said.But for residents like Melissa, every additional day underwater carries a cost. cards.headline: Cleanup begins near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach as floodwaters slowly recede
cards.teaser: Martin County pumping has allowed some residents to begin clearing flood-damaged homes. Recovery assistance is available at Hoke Library, and volunteers are planning a Nov. 25 fundraiser and meal.
cards.body:
Residents near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach have begun cleaning up their homes as Martin County pumping slowly lowers floodwaters that have stood for more than a week. The county began pumping Monday, allowing some homeowners to assess the damage, while other homes remained flooded.

Lisa French, her husband and several neighbors began removing damaged drywall, tearing out the kitchen and carrying ruined furniture and belongings into the front yard early Wednesday morning. Water had reached more than a foot deep in some rooms of her home. It has since receded, but much of what she owns has been destroyed. “You know, you’re sitting there with your house full of water, sitting in the fact that you lost your entire home. But now we can actually move and work instead of think,” French said.

Other residents were still waiting for the water to recede. Susan Destafney, who has lived in the neighborhood for four decades, described the flooding as unlike anything she had experienced there. “We’ve lived in our home for 40 years. We’ve never seen the likes of this,” Destafney said.

Martin County officials have opened a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach to connect flood victims with recovery assistance. Community volunteers have also been collecting cleaning supplies and other necessities for affected families. Alaura Macpherson, who runs the local group Quit Messen With Jensen, is organizing a community fundraiser and meal on Nov. 25 to raise money for flood victims. Local restaurants are expected to donate food. The event will also serve as a resource center connecting residents with contractors, cleanup services and other recovery assistance. “The community is what helps each other. We are a family,” Macpherson said.
