hero.headline: I-95 closed in both directions in Indian River County after pursuit, gunfire
hero.body:
Both directions of I-95 in Indian River County were closed early Friday following a pursuit and an exchange of gunfire between an FHP trooper and a suspect. The Indian River County Sheriff's Office said the highway was closed for the ongoing investigation.

Northbound drivers were being directed off I-95 at Indrio Road, while southbound drivers were being directed to exit at Oslo Road. The northbound entrance ramp from Indrio Road and the southbound entrance ramp at Oslo Road were also closed.

FHP said the shooting occurred around 11:20 p.m. near mile marker 141. The incident began when a trooper initiated a traffic stop and the suspect fled, prompting a pursuit, according to FHP. The pursuit escalated into an exchange of gunfire between the trooper and the suspect. FHP said the suspect sustained what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound and was pronounced dead at the scene.

FDLE will take over as the lead agency on the investigation. Officials said all body camera and dash camera video will be reviewed as part of the investigation.

hero.headline: Martin County moves to revive drainage project as Trailside flooding persists
hero.body:
Floodwater continues to cover parts of Trailside in western Martin County after a berm on county-owned land breached Monday, and the county is moving to revive a long-proposed project to drain water from the community. Residents described 3 to 4 feet of water covering parts of Hungryland Farms following last week's heavy rainfall.

Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said the berm breached on the Elise J Property northeast of Trailside, sending water into a nearby canal, with some flowing back into the community. High water has prevented crews from reaching the breach. Gorton plans to return Friday to assess the flooding and determine what immediate relief may be possible. “We're looking at ways to get the water out faster,” he said.

At Hungryland Farms, Melissa, who raises grass-fed cattle, said water kept rising after the rain stopped. Submerged pastures have left her cattle without their primary food source, forcing them to wade and swim in search of dry ground. She also pointed to a nearly submerged electrical transformer and questioned whether cattle could be electrocuted if they wandered too close. “It feels like Lake Okeechobee,” she said.

Trailside Homeowners Association President Kyla Shay raised drainage concerns in 2018. In a letter to homeowners that year, she warned that property south of Trailside had effectively become a reservoir, with water rising as much as 3.5 feet above community roads and breaching a berm. She also contacted the South Florida Water Management District, warning that blocked drainage had left some pastures under 8 feet of water. Shay said the underlying problems remained unresolved.

Gorton described Trailside as essentially a bathtub surrounded by berms, hundreds of acres of wetlands and two independent water control districts. Water enters the area but has only one drainage ditch through which to escape slowly.

Engineer Bob Higgins, who works with the Pal Mar Water Control District and the Hobe St. Lucie Conservancy District, said an outfall designed years ago would allow water to drain through the R G Mitigation Bank Preserve to the south and the neighboring Elise J property. Gorton said county officials discussed a water control structure with the property's former owner, and the former owners submitted two permit applications to the South Florida Water Management District.

Martin County acquired the property in 2026. Gorton said he has requested the original permit applications to help expedite approval and construction. “The good news is the county purchased that property, and it's our intent to bring that project forward,” he said.

hero.headline: Martin County seeks to revive drainage project as Trailside flooding persists
hero.body:
Floodwater continues to cover parts of Trailside in western Martin County after a berm breached on county-owned land Monday, sending water toward the community. County officials now plan to revive a previously unbuilt drainage project as residents contend with submerged pastures and drainage problems they warned about as far back as 2018.

Residents described 3 to 4 feet of water covering parts of Hungryland Farms, where cattle have been wading and swimming through flooded pastures in search of dry ground. The submerged grazing land has left the animals without their primary food source. Residents said water continued rising after last week's heavy rainfall stopped.

Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said the berm breached on the county-owned Elise J Property northeast of Trailside. Water entered a nearby canal, with some flowing back into the community. High water has prevented crews from reaching the breach, he said. Gorton described Trailside as essentially a bathtub, surrounded by berms, hundreds of acres of wetlands and two independent water control districts, with only one drainage ditch allowing water to escape slowly.

Trailside Homeowners Association President Kyla Shay warned homeowners in a 2018 letter that property south of the community had effectively become a reservoir. Water had risen as much as 3.5 feet above community roads and breached a berm. That year, she also contacted the South Florida Water Management District about blocked drainage that had left some pastures under 8 feet of water. “It's a combination of years of 'We'll get to it,' and we never got to it,” Shay said.

Engineer Bob Higgins, who works with the Pal Mar Water Control District and the Hobe St. Lucie Conservancy District, said an outfall had been designed years ago to drain water through the R G Mitigation Bank Preserve to the south and the neighboring Elise J property. Martin County acquired that property in 2026. Gorton said county officials had discussed a formal water control structure with the former owner, and the former owners submitted two permit applications to the South Florida Water Management District. Construction never began.

Gorton said he has requested the original permit applications to help expedite approval and construction. He also plans to return Friday to assess the flooding and possible immediate relief. “The good news is the county purchased that property, and it's our intent to bring that project forward,” he said.

cards.headline: Jensen Beach residents begin home cleanup as county pumping lowers floodwaters
cards.teaser: Some residents near Hyline Drive are clearing damaged homes while others remain flooded. Recovery assistance is available at Hoke Library in Jensen Beach.
cards.body:
Some residents near Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach have begun cleaning out their homes as Martin County pumping slowly lowers floodwaters that have stood in the neighborhood for more than a week. The county began pumping Monday, allowing some homeowners to assess the damage and start removing ruined belongings. Other residents are still waiting for the water to recede.

Lisa French, her husband and several neighbors began removing damaged drywall, tearing out the kitchen and carrying ruined furniture and belongings into the front yard early Wednesday morning. Water had reached more than a foot deep in some rooms of French’s home. It has since receded from the house, but much of what she owns has been destroyed. “You know, you’re sitting there with your house full of water, sitting in the fact that you lost your entire home. But now we can actually move and work instead of think,” French said.

Susan Destafney, who has lived in the neighborhood for four decades, is among the residents still waiting for floodwaters to recede. “We’ve lived in our home for 40 years. We’ve never seen the likes of this,” Destafney said. Community volunteers have been collecting cleaning supplies and other necessities for affected families, according to Alaura Macpherson, who runs the local group Quit Messen With Jensen.

Macpherson is also organizing a community fundraiser and meal on Nov. 25 to raise money for flood victims. Local restaurants are expected to donate food, and the event will serve as a resource center connecting residents with contractors, cleanup services and other recovery assistance. “The community is what helps each other. We are a family,” Macpherson said. Martin County officials have opened a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach to connect flood victims with recovery assistance.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce mother questions police response before daughter’s killing in Fort Lauderdale
hero.body:
A Fort Pierce mother has shared body-camera footage and is questioning whether officers could have done more to help her 19-year-old daughter before she was fatally shot near an Airbnb in Fort Lauderdale. Alacia Ford-Barron says the video shows her daughter, Myrah Zeigler, asking police for help before the shooting.

“I already knew half of what happened, and to see it and to hear it was heartbreaking,” Ford-Barron said. The footage shows officers arriving after an altercation involving two groups of women inside the Airbnb and telling everyone to leave. Ford-Barron says her daughter had been attacked and that belongings, including car keys, had been taken. The group needed to retrieve those items from a nearby park.

In the footage, Zeigler asks officers to walk with the group to get their belongings. An officer asks whether they have a way to get to the park, and Zeigler responds that they can. Ford-Barron says she believed officers were going to help.

Minutes later, gunfire erupts nearby, and an officer reports shots fired two blocks away. Friends can be heard screaming as officers try to revive Zeigler. She later died at a nearby hospital.

“I wanted to know why they didn't call backup. I wanted to know why she did not listen to my daughter when she was trying to explain to her and asking her to walk down to the park,” Ford-Barron said.

Larry Lamar Smith was later arrested in connection with Zeigler’s death. Ford-Barron says she appreciates the detectives’ work but still has questions about the initial police response. “I have to be my daughter's voice. I know that if I shut down, who's going to speak for my daughter?” she said.

hero.headline: Martin County firefighters union urges county to restore January hiring class
hero.body:
The Martin County Firefighters Union is asking county leaders to restore a January hiring class of about 25 firefighters that it says the county canceled, warning that existing staffing shortages could worsen as employees retire or leave. The union called on the Board of County Commissioners and county administrator to move forward with the class for Martin County Fire Rescue.

In a Facebook post, the union said the department is currently 17 firefighters short and could be about 25 short by January. It said fewer firefighters would mean fewer personnel available to respond to emergencies, greater reliance on mandatory and voluntary overtime, and increased demands on remaining crews. According to the union, the county cited budget concerns tied to Amendment 3 when canceling the class.

The union said its members recently agreed to forgo negotiating a new contract that would have taken effect in October, giving up a cost-of-living pay adjustment to help the county address financial challenges. Members made that concession after being assured that Fire Rescue would not be affected by hiring freezes tied to Amendment 3, the union said. The union also questioned county administrative pay increases, saying administrative employees received 6% raises in October while firefighters face staffing shortages.

In a statement, Martin County said it is taking a soft hiring freeze approach, evaluating vacancies and staffing needs as it reviews its long-term finances and operational needs. The county cited rising operating costs, inflation, potential revenue impacts following the passage of Amendment 3 and anticipated SAFER Grant repayment obligations in the upcoming budget cycle. It said the firefighter recruitment class was planned months before Amendment 3 passed, but current fiscal considerations prompted a review of future hiring. Maintaining public safety remains a county priority, the statement said.

hero.headline: Indian River County beaches recover after erosion; some access points remain closed
hero.body:
Indian River County beaches are beginning to recover after a nor’easter and king tides eroded the coastline, though some beach access points remain closed. At Tracking Station Beach, sand has begun shifting back into place after the beach experienced five to ten feet of erosion. Water levels there had risen almost as high as a sign, according to county erosion officials.

Johnnie Sabin, a coastal specialist with Indian River County’s Department of Natural Resources, said much of the sand placed on the beach has already begun returning. He said the beach and its berms are higher and wider, and credited dune plants with helping hold the sand together. The county’s Sector Five Beach Restoration Project performed as expected, he said. “Luckily because of the sand being there, it buffered all private properties, the roads, all the infrastructure we care about and it did its job,” Sabin said.

Major parks in the central beach area are open, and Sabin advised visitors to check the county’s website for access closures before heading out. The county plans to repair beach parks where needed. Beachgoer Erin Dobrinski said she had noticed erosion damage along the Sebastian riverfront, where part of a sidewalk was blocked off. The damage has not stopped her from enjoying the beach.

With more king tides expected, the county is closely monitoring the coast, Sabin said. He also reported that less than one percent of sea turtle nests were affected by the erosion. Erosion officials are asking visitors to help protect the shoreline by picking up trash and debris.

Waves and high water significantly impacted the county’s coastline. “This is a great example of coastal resistance at work,” officials said. Johnnie Sabin, a coastal specialist with Indian River County’s Department of Natural Resources, said the shoreline at Tracking Station Beach is already showing signs of recovery. “Much of the sand we placed on the beach, while it shifted briefly, has already been returning. I mean, these beaches, these berms, there's a lot more space. They're a little higher, a little wider so folks aren't in jeopardy to visit the beaches anymore,” Sabin said. Sabin explained that Tracking Station Beach experienced five to ten feet of erosion. He credited dune plants for helping hold the sand together and said the county’s Sector Five Beach Restoration Project performed as expected. “Luckily because of the sand being there, it buffered all private properties, the roads, all the infrastructure we care about and it did its job,” Sabin said. While major parks in the central beach area are open, some beach access points remain closed. Sabin advised visitors to check the county’s website before heading out. The county plans to repair beach parks where needed. Beachgoer Erin Dobrinski has noticed some of the damage but it's not stopping her from enjoying the beach. “You know down the Sebastian riverfront area down there there's a part of the sidewalk completely blocked off and if you peep around you can see it's all eroded,” Dobrinski said. Sabin said there are no current plans for another major sand project, but with more king tides expected, the county is closely monitoring the coast. There is good news for sea turtles, as Sabin reported that less than one percent of nests were affected by the erosion event. “They're resilient creatures. This is not their first rodeo. And they're going to continue doing what they do,” Sabin said. Erosion officials are asking the public to help protect the shoreline by picking up trash and debris. We are a family,” Macpherson said. Martin County officials have opened a Multi-Agency Resource Center at the Hoke Library in Jensen Beach to connect flood victims with recovery assistance. hero.headline: Port St. Lucie soccer stadium groundbreaking set for Dec. 12 at Walton & One
hero.body:
A groundbreaking ceremony for a new 6,000-seat soccer stadium at Walton & One in Port St. Lucie is scheduled for Dec. 12, the club announced Thursday. The club is preparing to compete in USL League One in 2027.

The development group will fully fund construction of the stadium, which will occupy approximately six acres. The group has entered into an agreement with the City of Port St. Lucie to use the land.

Plans call for the stadium to serve as a year-round destination for families and community members, with entertainment and other events in addition to soccer. “We set out to create something that feels like a true part of this community, a place where families can gather, young players can dream, and new traditions can take shape,” said club founder and CEO Gustavo Suárez.

The groundbreaking ceremony will begin at noon Dec. 12 and bring together club leaders, USL representatives, partners and founding members. A public celebration will follow at 1:30 p.m., with food trucks, entertainment and activities for all ages. The club says it will announce more event details in the coming weeks.

hero.headline: Martin County votes 3-2 to pursue quiet zones at three railroad crossings
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted 3-2 Tuesday to pursue train quiet zones at three initial crossings in Jensen Beach and Hobe Sound, reversing last year’s unanimous rejection. The decision followed complaints about train horns, with supporters citing quality of life and opponents raising safety concerns.

An initial motion called for turning all 27 railroad crossings in the county into quiet zones. A second motion narrowed the scope and passed. Work will begin with crossings at County Line Road and Skyline Drive in Jensen Beach, along with a third crossing along Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound near Mariner Sands.

Quiet-zone supporter Doug Farley described the disruption from train horns. “The horn all day and all night. And as I’m listening to that noisy disruption, I can visualize the intersection with four gates down, deployed, and cars safely behind them with that horn pointlessly bothering people,” Farley said.

The city of Stuart recently received a $1.86 million grant to enhance rail corridor safety. In Palm Beach County, Jupiter and Palm Beach Gardens recently established quiet zones.

The third is along Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound near Mariner Sands. The city of Stuart recently received a $1.86 million grant to enhance rail corridor safety. Lucie County has established a quiet zone in the southern end of the county at three crossings. In Palm Beach County, both Jupiter and Palm Beach Gardens recently set up quiet zones.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie leaders unanimously approve plans for 6,000-seat soccer stadium
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie leaders voted unanimously to move forward with plans for a 6,000-seat stadium that will be home to the Port St. Lucie Soccer Club. The proposal combines a soccer venue with space for concerts, festivals and community events throughout the year. City officials approved plans for a two-story stadium on a property that will also include a bar, a restaurant and retail shops. The unanimous vote advances a project planned for both sports and entertainment, with soccer games among the activities the venue will host. All city leaders voting on the plans supported moving forward.

The stadium plans call for 6,000 seats across a two-story facility. In addition to the stadium itself, the planned property includes places to eat, drink and shop. A restaurant, bar and retail stores are part of the proposal approved by city leaders. Those businesses are planned alongside a venue whose uses will extend beyond soccer matches. The project brings the stadium and the other planned establishments together on the same property. The approved plans therefore cover both the sports facility and the restaurant, bar and retail components, rather than a stadium alone.

For soccer, the venue will provide a home for the Port St. Lucie Soccer Club, identified in the plans as a USL League One team. The club’s games will be one of the stadium’s main uses, alongside its schedule of other events. The planned capacity is 6,000 seats, and the stadium is designed as a two-story building. While the club will call the venue home, the proposal is not limited to hosting its matches. The same stadium is also planned to accommodate entertainment and community gatherings, making soccer one part of the year-round use described for the property.

Concerts, festivals and community events are all included in the plans approved by city officials. Those activities will share the venue with soccer, giving the stadium a role beyond serving as the club’s home ground. The proposal calls for events throughout the year rather than soccer games alone. Together, the planned uses encompass sports, live music, festivals and local gatherings. With the unanimous approval, leaders have agreed to advance plans for a 6,000-seat venue that combines those activities with a bar, restaurant and retail shops on the property. The stadium’s planned role remains both a soccer home and a year-round event venue.
